title: Kubernetes Headless Service
question: Most Services hand out one address and share traffic between the Pods behind it. A Headless Service does not. What do you get instead, and when is that what you want?
technical: A normal Service has a stable virtual IP and load-balances traffic across ready Pods.
A Headless Service uses clusterIP: None. Kubernetes does not create the normal virtual Service IP.
DNS returns individual Pod endpoint addresses, allowing clients to discover or connect to a specific Pod.
layman: A normal Service is a company’s main telephone number. A Headless Service gives callers the direct numbers of individual employees.
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: database-service
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: database
  ports:
    - port: 5432
      targetPort: 5432
followups: Does it perform normal Service load balancing?
Why is it often used with StatefulSets?
What DNS records are returned?
redflags: Says it exposes Pods directly to the internet
Says it means a Service without Pods
memory: Headless = no virtual Service IP; DNS exposes individual Pod endpoints.

title: Kubernetes Service Definitions
question: Pods come and go, and their IP addresses go with them. So how does anything find them? Explain what a Service does and the types you can choose from.
technical: Pods are replaceable and their IP addresses change. A Service gives a stable network identity to Pods selected by labels.
ClusterIP is internal-only. NodePort opens a port on every node. LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer. ExternalName creates a DNS alias.
port is the Service-facing port; targetPort is the application port on the Pod.
layman: Pods are employees who change desks. A Service is the permanent reception number that stays unchanged.
usecases: Public or private load-balanced TCP services
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: subscription-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: subscription-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
followups: Difference between port and targetPort?
What if the selector is wrong?
Service versus Ingress?
redflags: Uses NodePort as the default public endpoint
memory: Service = stable endpoint in front of replaceable Pods.

title: Production Delivery Pipeline
question: Walk me through how code gets from a developer's commit to running in production. What does a pipeline you would actually trust look like?
technical: Validate code through pull-request review, linting, unit, integration and contract tests.
Run static security analysis, dependency, secret, licence, infrastructure and container-image scans, and generate an SBOM.
Build one immutable artefact and promote the same artefact through environments.
Use backward-compatible database migrations, controlled rollout, health verification and automated rollback thresholds.
layman: A delivery pipeline is a factory line. Every product passes quality and safety checks before customers receive it.
usecases: Canary or blue-green deployment to GKE or Cloud Run
code:
Commit
  -> Pull request checks
  -> Tests and security scans
  -> Build immutable image
  -> Push to Artifact Registry
  -> Deploy to test
  -> Smoke and integration tests
  -> Canary production deployment
  -> Promote or roll back
followups: Why promote the same artefact?
Where are secrets stored?
How are database migrations handled?
What triggers rollback?
What if the application deploy succeeds but the database migration fails?
How are production approvals controlled?
memory: Build once, test thoroughly, promote safely and verify continuously.

title: Kubernetes Routing
question: Someone types your URL into a browser. Follow that request all the way until it reaches a Pod.
technical: A common route is user → DNS → cloud load balancer → Ingress or Gateway → Service → ready Pod → container.
Layer 4 routing uses IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. Layer 7 routing understands hostnames, URL paths, methods, headers and cookies.
Internal services use Kubernetes DNS names, such as payment-service.finance.svc.cluster.local.
layman: A parcel reaches the right city, building, department and finally an available employee.
code:
Internet
  -> DNS
  -> HTTPS Load Balancer
  -> Ingress / Gateway
  -> Kubernetes Service
  -> Ready Pod
  -> Container port
followups: Ingress versus Service?
Where is TLS terminated?
What if there are no ready endpoints?
memory: Routing narrows traffic from DNS to load balancer to route to Service to Pod.

title: Kubernetes Nodes
question: What is a node in Kubernetes, and what is it doing for you?
technical: A node is a worker machine, usually a VM in GKE, that runs Pods.
The kubelet ensures assigned Pods run; the container runtime runs containers; networking components connect Pods and Services.
Node pools group similar machines. Labels, affinity, taints and tolerations control workload placement.
The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled and removes underused nodes when safe.
layman: A node is an apartment building. Pods are residents, and the control plane assigns them to buildings.
code:
Node pool: encoding-pool
Label: workload=encoding
Taint: workload=encoding:NoSchedule

Encoding Pods:
- match the label
- tolerate the taint
followups: What happens when a node fails?
Pod autoscaling versus node autoscaling?
Why separate node pools?
redflags: Says node and Pod are the same
memory: Node = worker machine; node pool = group of similar workers.

title: Kubernetes Pods
question: Why does Kubernetes wrap containers in Pods instead of just running the containers on their own?
technical: A Pod is Kubernetes’ smallest deployable unit and contains one or more tightly coupled containers.
Containers share one IP, port namespace, mounted volumes and lifecycle; they communicate through localhost.
Most Pods contain one main application container. Sidecars and init containers are used only for tightly related functions.
Pods are temporary; important state should not rely on local Pod storage.
layman: A Pod is an office room shared by a main worker and, sometimes, a closely related assistant.
code:
Pod
├── application container
├── optional sidecar
├── shared network
├── shared volumes
└── common lifecycle
followups: Can two containers use the same port?
Pod versus Deployment?
What happens to local data after replacement?
memory: Pod = smallest temporary deployment unit, usually one application container.

title: Deployment YAML Configuration
question: Open a Deployment YAML with me. Which fields matter, and which ones would you insist on seeing before this goes near production?
technical: replicas defines Pod count. selector must match Pod-template labels. strategy controls rollout.
Resource requests guide scheduling; limits cap usage. Readiness controls traffic; liveness detects a stuck process; startup protects slow starts.
Use immutable images, a dedicated service account, non-root execution, no privilege escalation and graceful termination.
A complete setup also needs Service, HPA, PodDisruptionBudget, NetworkPolicy, monitoring and external secret management.
layman: Deployment YAML is an instruction sheet describing what to run, how many copies to keep and how to replace them safely.
code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: subscription-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: subscription-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: subscription-api
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: subscription-api
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: asia-docker.pkg.dev/project/app/subscription-api:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: "1"
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: 8080
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health/live
              port: 8080
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
followups: Why not use latest?
Readiness versus liveness?
Meaning of maxUnavailable: 0?
How are secrets supplied?
memory: Deployment YAML defines desired replicas, rollout, resources, health and security.

title: DaemonSets
question: What is a DaemonSet, and when is it the right thing to reach for?
technical: A DaemonSet runs one Pod on every eligible node, or every node matching scheduling conditions.
When a matching node joins, Kubernetes adds the DaemonSet Pod automatically.
It is intended for node-level agents, not ordinary business application scaling.
layman: A DaemonSet assigns one security guard to every building. New buildings automatically receive a guard.
code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-agent
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-agent
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: agent
          image: example/log-agent:2.1.0
followups: What happens when a node is added?
How do you target only GPU nodes?
Risks of hostPath mounts?
redflags: Uses DaemonSet for a normal API
Says one Pod in the entire cluster
memory: DaemonSet = one node-level Pod on every eligible node.

title: Private GKE VPC Cluster
question: Your GKE cluster has no public endpoint. So how do users reach the apps, how do admins reach the cluster, and how do Pods reach the internet?
technical: Private GKE nodes use internal IP addresses and do not need public node IPs.
Control-plane access should use a private endpoint or tightly restricted authorised networks.
Cloud NAT provides controlled internet egress; Private Google Access supports Google APIs; Workload Identity replaces service-account keys.
Public applications can still use an external HTTPS Load Balancer, Cloud Armor and GKE Ingress while nodes remain private.
layman: The office has no doors opening directly to the street. Visitors use a guarded entrance and employees use a controlled exit.
code:
Internet users
  -> External HTTPS Load Balancer
  -> Cloud Armor
  -> GKE Ingress / Gateway
  -> Private GKE Pods

Administrators
  -> Identity + MFA
  -> VPN or IAP
  -> Private control-plane endpoint

Private nodes
  -> Cloud NAT
  -> Approved external services
followups: How do nodes reach the internet?
How do administrators reach the API?
How do Pods access Secret Manager?
memory: Private GKE keeps nodes private while controlled gateways handle ingress, admin and egress.

title: Bastion Host
question: What is a bastion host, and how do you stop it from becoming the easiest way into your network?
technical: A bastion or jump host is a controlled administration entry point for private resources.
Prefer Identity-Aware Proxy, OS Login, MFA and short-lived privileges; a public IP is often unnecessary.
Use least privilege, strong patching, complete access logging, restricted network reach and no stored long-lived credentials.
It is for administration, not normal application traffic.
layman: A bastion is a guarded reception desk where visitors prove their identity before entering secure rooms.
code:
Administrator
  -> Enterprise identity + MFA
  -> Identity-Aware Proxy
  -> Private bastion / VM
  -> Approved internal resource
followups: Does it require a public IP?
How do you audit actions?
What if it is compromised?
memory: Bastion = controlled administrative doorway, ideally identity-based and private.

title: Shipping Logs
question: Your application and Kubernetes logs are scattered across dozens of nodes. How do you get them all into one place?
technical: Applications normally emit structured logs to stdout and stderr. A node or platform agent forwards them to Cloud Logging or a SIEM.
Agents include Google Cloud Ops Agent, Fluent Bit and OpenTelemetry Collector.
Include service, version, severity, trace ID, safe tenant context, operation and error category. Redact secrets and sensitive data.
Collectors should buffer and retry during temporary failure, but business requests should not fail merely because logging is unavailable.
layman: Every branch writes a diary, and a courier sends all diaries to one central office.
code:
{
  "severity": "ERROR",
  "service": "subscription-api",
  "version": "1.4.2",
  "traceId": "4ad7c98c",
  "tenantId": "tenant-123",
  "operation": "create-subscription",
  "errorCode": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "durationMs": 2450
}
followups: Why stdout?
What if the logging platform fails?
How do you prevent sensitive-data leakage?
memory: Write structured logs locally; agents reliably forward them centrally.

title: Centralised Log Monitoring
question: Everyone says they have centralised logging, but often they just have a big pile of log files. What is the real difference?
technical: Centralised monitoring combines logs from applications, infrastructure and environments in one controlled platform.
Storage preserves records. Monitoring adds search, correlation, dashboards, alerting, retention, access control and incident integration.
Alerts should indicate meaningful user or business impact and include severity, context, owner and runbook.
layman: Keeping CCTV recordings is logging. A security team watching for unusual activity and raising alarms is monitoring.
code:
Good alert:
Subscription creation failures > 5%
for 10 minutes
and affected requests > 100

Poor alert:
One ERROR log occurred
followups: What makes an alert actionable?
How do you avoid alert fatigue?
How do logs relate to metrics and traces?
redflags: Cannot distinguish logs, metrics and traces
memory: Central monitoring turns stored events into searchable evidence and actionable alerts.

title: Compute Engine Virtual Machines
question: When would you put something on a plain VM with Compute Engine instead of GKE, Cloud Run or Cloud Functions?
technical: Compute Engine is Google Cloud’s IaaS VM platform. The customer controls the OS, software, machine type, disks and runtime configuration.
Use it for legacy applications, vendor appliances, specialised OS or kernel requirements, lift-and-shift and workloads needing low-level machine control.
For production, use managed instance groups, load balancing, health checks, autoscaling, instance templates, private IPs, Shielded VMs, OS Login, patching and backups.
Prefer Cloud Run for stateless managed containers and GKE when Kubernetes orchestration is justified.
layman: Compute Engine is an empty rented office you must furnish and maintain. Cloud Run is more like a serviced meeting room.
code:
Compute Engine: full VM and OS control
GKE: Kubernetes container platform
Cloud Run: serverless stateless containers
Cloud Functions: event-driven functions
followups: What is a managed instance group?
How do you make VMs highly available?
When is Cloud Run better?
redflags: One VM for a critical service
memory: Compute Engine = full VM control; prefer managed platforms when suitable.

title: GCP vs AWS VPC Differences
question: You have built networks on AWS and now you are on Google Cloud. What is genuinely different about how VPCs work here?
technical: A Google Cloud VPC is global; its subnets are regional. One VPC can contain subnets across several regions.
An AWS VPC is regional; its subnets are scoped to individual Availability Zones.
AWS uses stateful Security Groups on interfaces and stateless subnet Network ACLs. GCP uses VPC firewall rules and hierarchical policies.
GCP Shared VPC supports centrally managed networks across projects. AWS commonly uses shared VPC resources and Transit Gateway hub designs.
layman: A GCP VPC can be one company network with offices in several regions. An AWS VPC is usually one regional company network connected to other regional networks.
usecases: Regional AWS VPCs connected through Transit Gateway
code:
GCP global VPC
  ├── Singapore regional subnet
  ├── Tokyo regional subnet
  └── London regional subnet

AWS
  Singapore regional VPC
  Tokyo regional VPC
  London regional VPC
  -> connect through peering / Transit Gateway
followups: Is a GCP subnet global?
Security Group versus NACL?
Is peering transitive?
How does NAT differ?
memory: GCP VPC global and subnet regional; AWS VPC regional and subnet AZ-scoped.

title: Designing for Highest Throughput
question: What is the difference between throughput and latency, and how would you build something that handles a lot of traffic?
technical: Throughput is work completed per unit of time; latency is the duration of one operation.
Increase throughput using horizontal scaling, partitioning, parallel processing, batching, queues, connection pooling, caching and efficient serialisation.
Use bounded concurrency and backpressure. Unlimited concurrency can cause contention, retries, memory pressure and lower throughput.
First find the real bottleneck: CPU, disk, network, database locks, connection limits, hot partitions or external rate limits.
layman: Throughput is the number of cars passing through a toll plaza each hour. Latency is how long one car takes.
code:
Producer
  -> partitioned durable queue
  -> bounded parallel consumers
  -> batch writes
  -> backpressure
  -> autoscaling using backlog age
followups: Can more concurrency reduce throughput?
What is backpressure?
How do you maintain ordering?
How do you locate the bottleneck?
memory: Throughput = volume over time; optimise the real bottleneck with bounded parallelism.

title: BigQuery Partitioning and Clustering
question: Your BigQuery bill is climbing because every query reads the whole table. Explain partitioning and clustering, and when you would use both.
technical: Partitioning divides a table into segments, usually by date, timestamp, ingestion time or integer range. Queries can scan only relevant partitions.
Clustering organises data within the table or partition by selected columns so BigQuery can skip irrelevant storage blocks.
A common multi-tenant event design is partition by event date and cluster by tenant ID and event type.
Choose fields from actual query patterns, require partition filters on large tables, monitor bytes scanned and use partition expiry for retention.
layman: Partitioning puts books from each year in separate rooms. Clustering arranges the books inside each room by customer or subject.
code:
CREATE TABLE analytics.events
PARTITION BY DATE(event_timestamp)
CLUSTER BY tenant_id, event_type
AS SELECT * FROM source_events;

SELECT *
FROM analytics.events
WHERE DATE(event_timestamp) = '2026-07-28'
  AND tenant_id = 'tenant-123'
  AND event_type = 'SUBSCRIPTION_CREATED';
followups: Why not partition by every tenant?
What is partition pruning?
How are late events handled?
How do you enforce retention?
redflags: One partition per tenant by default
memory: Partition broadly, then cluster selectively inside each partition.

title: Validate Claimed Production Scale
question: Your CV says you led backend engineering for a platform with over three million daily users. Take me through it: what the architecture looked like, what was yours to own, how much traffic at peak, what you promised on speed and uptime, and the worst incident you had to handle.
technical: Separate the scale of the full product from the services personally owned.
Provide measurable values such as peak RPS, concurrency, p95/p99 latency, error rate, processing volume and unit cost.
Explain topology, autoscaling, cache/CDN use, database limits, dependencies and incident controls.
State which architecture and operational decisions were made personally and how improvement was verified.
layman: Do not accept “the company had millions of users”. The candidate must explain exactly what they built and how they measured it.
usecases: Validate real ownership of a high-scale media, subscription or recommendation service.
code:
Interview focus:
- Scale claims require scope, metrics, failures and personal decisions.
followups: What was the highest measured RPS?
Which dashboard proved the SLO?
What failed during peak traffic?
redflags: Claims ownership of the entire platform without component detail
memory: Scale claims require scope, metrics, failures and personal decisions.

title: Legacy-to-Microservices Migration
question: Tell me about a legacy system you broke apart into microservices. How did you decide where the lines went, what did you do about the data, how did you keep it safe, and how did you know it was better afterwards?
technical: Start with a measurable business or operational problem, not a preference for microservices.
Identify bounded contexts and business capabilities rather than technical layers.
Use an incremental strangler approach, explicit contracts, feature flags and gradual traffic movement.
Move towards service-owned data using outbox, CDC or controlled backfill; avoid uncontrolled shared-table access.
Compare deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, MTTR, latency, availability and cost before and after.
layman: Renovate a building room by room while people continue using it, rather than demolishing everything in one day.
usecases: Extract subscription management from a media monolith while old and new paths coexist.
code:
Interview focus:
- A migration is successful only when business and engineering outcomes improve.
followups: Why was each boundary chosen?
How were cross-service transactions handled?
What remained in the monolith?
memory: A migration is successful only when business and engineering outcomes improve.

title: Production-Grade AI Platform on GCP
question: A client wants an assistant that answers questions from their private documents, shows where each answer came from, and serves a lot of people at once. Design it on GCP.
technical: Use an authenticated frontend and API layer on Cloud Run or GKE with tenant-aware authorisation.
Ingest through Cloud Storage, asynchronous processing, parsing/OCR, chunking, embeddings and a vector index with metadata ACL filters.
Use Vertex AI Gemini for grounded generation, citations and abstention when evidence is insufficient.
Add Workload Identity, Secret Manager, encryption, Cloud Armor, VPC controls, observability, evaluation, audit and deletion.
Version model, prompt, embeddings, chunking, index and evaluation dataset as one release configuration.
layman: It is a secure company librarian that searches only the books you are allowed to read and shows exactly where the answer came from.
usecases: Enterprise document assistant for policy and support knowledge.
code:
Interview focus:
- RAG production design is retrieval, authorisation, evaluation and operations—not only an LLM call.
followups: Where is document ACL enforced?
How is prompt injection handled?
How is a tenant deleted?
redflags: Sends all documents to the model
memory: RAG production design is retrieval, authorisation, evaluation and operations—not only an LLM call.

title: Production GKE Platform
question: You have about 40 microservices to run. Design a GKE platform that is secure and stays up.
technical: Use a regional private cluster, multiple zones, dedicated service accounts and Workload Identity.
Configure requests and limits, readiness/liveness/startup probes, HPA, PodDisruptionBudgets and topology spread.
Use NetworkPolicies, pod security, Secret Manager integration and controlled ingress.
Adopt progressive delivery, controlled upgrades, backup/restore testing and central observability.
layman: A well-run apartment complex has several buildings, backup utilities, security checkpoints and rules preventing one resident from consuming everything.
usecases: Enterprise microservice platform with public APIs and internal workers.
code:
Interview focus:
- Production GKE requires workload, network, identity, upgrade and failure controls.
followups: Autopilot or Standard and why?
What happens when a zone fails?
How are upgrades performed?
memory: Production GKE requires workload, network, identity, upgrade and failure controls.

title: Reliable Event-Driven Payments or Credentials
question: Design a message-driven flow where nothing can be lost and nothing can happen twice. No missed orders, no double payments.
technical: Assume at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent.
Write business state and an outbox record in one transaction, then publish asynchronously.
Use a unique event ID and inbox/processed-event record with a unique database constraint.
Acknowledge only after durable completion; use bounded backoff, DLQ and replay through the same idempotent path.
Reuse the same idempotency key with external providers and reconcile uncertain outcomes.
layman: The courier may deliver the instruction twice, so the office stamps each request number and performs it only once.
code:
Interview focus:
- At-least-once delivery plus durable idempotency prevents duplicate business action.
followups: What if DB commit succeeds but acknowledgement fails?
How is replay safe?
How is ordering handled?
memory: At-least-once delivery plus durable idempotency prevents duplicate business action.

title: Idempotent Paid-Subscription API
question: You expose an API that starts a paid subscription. The client times out and retries. How do you make sure the customer is not signed up, or charged, twice?
technical: Require a client idempotency key scoped to tenant or customer and store it durably.
Store a request fingerprint, operation state, resource ID and original response.
Use a unique constraint so one concurrent request owns the operation.
Reuse the same key with the payment provider and reject reuse with a different request body.
Add business uniqueness constraints, reconciliation, audit, authorisation and rate limiting.
Classify operations as safe, idempotent or non-idempotent, and have clients retry with bounded backoff and jitter.
layman: A ticket number identifies one purchase. Showing the same ticket again returns the same result instead of charging again.
code:
Interview focus:
- Idempotency must cover the API, database and payment provider.
followups: What if payment succeeds but the local write fails?
How long are keys retained?
What if two different keys create the same plan?
How are simultaneous retries handled?
memory: Idempotency must cover the API, database and payment provider.

title: Major Production Incident Leadership
question: Tell me about the worst production incident you personally led. What did you do in the first 15 minutes, and what changed for good afterwards?
technical: Declare severity, establish a channel and assign incident command.
Assess business impact and stabilise before extended root-cause analysis.
Freeze unrelated changes, inspect RED metrics and use rollback, feature flags, load shedding or degradation.
Give regular stakeholder updates and preserve a timeline.
Verify recovery and monitor for recurrence before standing down.
Complete a blameless review with corrective actions, owners, due dates, tests, alerts and runbook updates.
layman: During a fire, first protect people and stop the fire spreading; investigate the exact ignition source after the building is stable.
usecases: Latency spike after deployment caused by an expensive query and connection-pool exhaustion.
code:
Interview focus:
- Incident leadership means stabilise, communicate, learn and prevent recurrence.
followups: What decision did you personally make?
How was customer impact measured?
Which actions remain open?
What is the communication cadence?
Who may authorise rollback?
memory: Incident leadership means stabilise, communicate, learn and prevent recurrence.

title: Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore and Bigtable
question: Cloud SQL, Spanner, Firestore, Bigtable. When is each one the right pick, and when is each one a mistake?
technical: Cloud SQL suits relational transactions at moderate scale but needs connection, capacity and failover planning.
Spanner suits globally scalable relational workloads with strong consistency but costs more and requires careful key design.
Firestore suits document-oriented and real-time applications with planned query patterns.
Bigtable suits very high-throughput key or time-series access, not relational joins and general transactions.
layman: Choose the correct storage cabinet for the shape of the information and how it must be retrieved.
usecases: Subscriptions in Cloud SQL, global strongly consistent records in Spanner, user settings in Firestore and telemetry in Bigtable.
code:
Interview focus:
- Choose data services from consistency, query, scale and operational requirements.
followups: Which service for a financial ledger?
How do access patterns change the choice?
redflags: No discussion of consistency or transactions
memory: Choose data services from consistency, query, scale and operational requirements.

title: Media Upload and Encoding Pipeline
question: Users upload video. You need different quality versions, subtitles, thumbnails and DRM. Design the pipeline.
technical: Use signed or resumable direct upload to object storage, checksum validation and quarantine.
Trigger an idempotent asynchronous workflow through Pub/Sub or a workflow engine.
Track explicit job states and run independent renditions in parallel with bounded retries and DLQ.
Publish the final manifest only after required outputs succeed; use CDN, lifecycle policies and cost/quality metrics.
layman: A film enters a factory where separate stations create HD, mobile, subtitles and thumbnails. It is published only after required stations pass.
code:
Interview focus:
- Large media processing should be direct-uploaded, asynchronous, stateful and idempotent.
followups: How do you avoid encoding the same source three times?
How do you recover partially completed work?
memory: Large media processing should be direct-uploaded, asynchronous, stateful and idempotent.

title: Validate Cost-Reduction Claims
question: You say you cut infrastructure cost. How did you work out the saving, and how did you prove the system had not become slower or less reliable?
technical: Show before-and-after cost by compute, storage, egress, licences and operations.
Normalise for traffic and report unit cost such as cost per user, request or encoded minute.
Include engineering and migration cost and disclose operational trade-offs.
Verify SLO, latency and load-test results before declaring success.
layman: A cheaper delivery company is not truly cheaper if it loses parcels or takes twice as long.
usecases: Compare an Aspera replacement or GKE migration using unit economics.
code:
Interview focus:
- Cost improvement must be normalised and balanced against reliability and performance.
followups: Was traffic equal in both periods?
Was redundancy reduced?
What hidden support cost appeared?
redflags: Quotes a percentage without baseline numbers
memory: Cost improvement must be normalised and balanced against reliability and performance.

title: Multi-Tenant Cloud Security
question: Several clients share one application on GCP and their data is sensitive. How do you keep it secure?
technical: Classify data and use least-privilege IAM, Workload Identity, Secret Manager and encryption.
Enforce tenant authorisation at identity, application and data layers.
Use private networking, Cloud Armor, audit logs, vulnerability management, backups and retention/deletion controls.
Use just-in-time approved and audited privileged access, never a shared permanent admin account.
layman: Each customer has a locked room in the same building, and staff receive only time-limited access to rooms they must service.
code:
Interview focus:
- Tenant security requires identity, data, network, key and operational isolation.
followups: How is emergency database access granted?
How are tenant restores performed?
How are keys rotated?
memory: Tenant security requires identity, data, network, key and operational isolation.

title: Production Observability and SRE
question: Before you let a service go live, what dashboards and alerts do you insist are already there?
technical: Use RED metrics: request rate, errors and duration, plus saturation and dependency health.
Add business transaction metrics, queue backlog and DLQ, database connections, deployment markers and synthetic checks.
Use structured logs, correlation IDs and distributed traces.
Maintain SLO and error-budget dashboards with actionable burn-rate alerts linked to runbooks.
layman: A car dashboard needs speed, fuel, warning lights and engine temperature—not only whether the engine is switched on.
usecases: Production API dashboard with p95 latency, success rate, dependency latency and release markers.
code:
Interview focus:
- Observe user outcomes, dependencies, saturation and SLO burn.
followups: Which alerts should page a human?
How is missing telemetry detected?
memory: Observe user outcomes, dependencies, saturation and SLO burn.

title: Agentic Refund Workflow
question: Design an agent that reads a support request, looks up the customer, suggests a refund, and only pays out once a human agrees.
technical: Use deterministic workflow steps for critical operations and model reasoning only where flexibility is needed.
Define typed tools and enforce identity, tenant and permission in application code.
Separate read and write tools, apply least privilege and require human approval before financial action.
Persist state, enforce step, time and token limits, use idempotency and audit every decision and tool call.
layman: The assistant may recommend a refund, but a controlled cashier system verifies authority and requires approval before money moves.
code:
Interview focus:

title: Prevent Double Booking Under Extreme Contention
question: Two million users open at 12:00 for five thousand seats. Two of them tap seat A1 in the same millisecond. How do you guarantee the seat is sold exactly once — and why is "check if free, then book" wrong?
technical: "Read then write" is a check-then-act race: both requests read free before either writes. The fix is to make claiming the seat a single atomic operation, so the loser is told no by the system rather than by a refund.

Admission control first. A virtual waiting room issues signed queue tokens and admits a bounded number of users into the booking path; the rest hold a position. This protects the database from two million concurrent sessions competing for five thousand rows.

Short-lived hold. SET seat:{show}:{seat} {holdId} NX EX 300 claims the seat atomically — NX means the second tap simply fails. Release with a Lua compare-and-delete so a slow request cannot delete a hold that has already expired and been re-issued to someone else.

The database is the source of truth. Redis is throughput, not correctness: a failover can lose holds. Enforce UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id) on confirmed bookings, and confirm with a conditional write — UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'HELD' AND hold_id = $1 — so a lost hold degrades to a rejected booking, never a duplicate one.

Make payment idempotent on the hold id, and define the compensation path: if payment settles after the hold expired and the seat was resold, auto-refund and notify. At this scale that case is rare but never zero, so it needs an owner, not an assumption.
layman: You do not ask whether a seat is free and then sit down. You put your coat on it the moment you choose it — and only one coat fits. If you never come back, the coat is removed and the seat returns to the room.
usecases: Ticketing, cinema and travel seat maps
Any finite inventory with a burst of demand
code:
-- atomic claim (Redis): only one caller can succeed
SET seat:show42:A1 hold_9f3 NX EX 300

-- safe release: delete only if the hold is still mine
-- EVAL "if redis.call('get',KEYS[1])==ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del',KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" 1 seat:show42:A1 hold_9f3

-- durable truth: the database refuses the duplicate even if Redis failed over
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX booked_once ON bookings (show_id, seat_id)
  WHERE status = 'BOOKED';

UPDATE seats SET status = 'BOOKED', booking_id = $2
WHERE show_id = $3 AND seat_id = $4
  AND status = 'HELD' AND hold_id = $1;   -- 0 rows updated = lost the race
followups: Redis fails over and loses the hold keys. What still stops the double booking?
Payment succeeds after the five-minute hold expired. What happens to the user and the seat?
Why not SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat row for every request?
How do you stop bots from holding the whole seat map for five minutes at a time?

Treats a Redis lock as the guarantee and puts no constraint in the database
Holds a database transaction open for the duration of the payment
Has no answer for expired holds, refunds, or the payment/hold race
memory: Claim atomically, hold briefly, confirm conditionally — Redis for throughput, a unique constraint for truth.

title: Expire Ephemeral Content Without a Cron Job
question: Design Stories that disappear after 24 hours for two billion users. A cron job running DELETE FROM stories WHERE expires_at < NOW() is not acceptable — what do you do instead?
technical: Separate visibility from reclamation. Correctness comes from the read path: every query carries AND expires_at > NOW(), so a story becomes invisible the exact second it expires regardless of when its bytes are removed. No job can be late.

Reclaim space at the storage layer, where the engine already walks the data: native row TTL in Cassandra, DynamoDB or Scylla; EXPIRE on the Redis feed keys; and an object-lifecycle rule on S3/GCS for the media, which is the bulk of the bytes.

In a relational store, partition by day and DROP or DETACH the whole partition after a grace window. Dropping a partition is a catalogue operation; deleting its rows one by one writes every row to the WAL, bloats the table, and stalls replicas.

Index correctly: a partial index cannot use NOW() (Postgres requires an IMMUTABLE predicate), so use a composite (author_id, expires_at DESC) per partition and let partition pruning skip expired days entirely.
TTL is eventual, so bound the grace window and keep a real deletion path for takedowns and GDPR erasure — "hidden on read" is not "erased", and an auditor will ask for proof of the second one.
layman: A cinema does not send staff to tear down every expired poster at midnight. The poster carries its own date, the ushers stop pointing at it, and the cleaning crew clears the wall on its normal round.
usecases: Stories, disappearing messages and ephemeral media
Time-boxed offers, OTPs and share links
Any table where rows outnumber the reads that touch them
code:
-- 1. read path decides visibility (a late cleanup can never leak a story)
SELECT id, media_url
FROM stories
WHERE author_id = ANY($1) AND expires_at > NOW()
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

-- 2. daily partition; reclaim with DDL, not DELETE
CREATE TABLE stories_2026_08_24 PARTITION OF stories
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-08-24') TO ('2026-08-25');
DROP TABLE stories_2026_08_24;   -- instant, no WAL storm, no replica lag

-- 3. storage-layer TTL does the rest
-- Cassandra:  INSERT INTO stories (...) VALUES (...) USING TTL 86400;
-- DynamoDB:   enable TTL on the expires_at attribute (epoch seconds)
-- Redis feed: SET story:123 <payload> EX 86400
-- S3 media:   lifecycle rule -> Expiration: Days: 1
followups: Why does a nightly bulk DELETE hurt replicas and autovacuum?
The row is hidden but still on disk — how do you answer a GDPR erasure request?
Cassandra TTL leaves tombstones. What breaks if compaction falls behind?
Clocks differ between app and database. Whose NOW() decides expiry?
redflags: Reaches for a cron job or a scheduler as the first and only answer
Deletes rows to expire them, then argues about batch size instead of dropping partitions
Assumes TTL is a compliance-grade deletion guarantee
Proposes a partial index on NOW(), or forgets the expiry predicate on the read path
memory: Hide on read, reclaim on write: predicate for correctness, TTL and partition DROP for space.

title: Tenant-Aware Rate Limiting and Quotas
question: How do you stop one customer using up all the capacity, while keeping the limits fair and predictable for everyone else?
technical: Enforce limits per tenant, not per instance: a shared token bucket keyed by tenant ID in a fast store such as Redis, checked at the gateway before expensive work starts.
Layer the limits: burst rate per second, sustained daily quota and concurrency caps, with tier-specific values stored as tenant configuration.
Return 429 with Retry-After and publish usage metrics so tenants can see consumption before they hit the wall.

Known issues: per-pod in-memory counters undercount as replicas scale, a single global limit lets one large tenant starve small ones, and hard cutoffs break tenant batch jobs — offer queueing or degradation for lower tiers.
Exempt or separately pool internal platform traffic so system jobs never consume tenant quota.
layman: A gym gives every member their own swipe allowance instead of counting people at the door — one heavy user cannot book every machine, and premium members get more sessions.
code:
def allow(tenant, cost=1):
    key = f"rl:{tenant.id}:{now_minute()}"
    used = redis.incrby(key, cost)      # shared across all gateways
    redis.expire(key, 120)
    return used <= LIMITS[tenant.tier].per_minute
followups: Fixed window, sliding window or token bucket — and why?
How are limits enforced consistently across many gateway replicas?
If the limiter store is down, do you fail open or closed?
How do tenants discover their remaining quota?

Per-pod in-memory counters treated as accurate
Rate limiting applied after the expensive work already ran

title: Schema Migrations Across Thousands of Tenants
question: You have 5,000 tenant schemas that all need the same change. How do you roll it out without breaking anyone, and what goes wrong at that scale?
technical: Treat it as a fleet rollout, not a single migration: an orchestrator tracks per-tenant schema version, migrates in batches and records success or failure per tenant.
Canary on internal and low-risk tenants first, and use expand-and-contract so application code tolerates both old and new schema during the window.
Accept a long mixed-version window: with thousands of schemas the fleet is never on one version at the same moment, so code must handle version skew.
Known issues: table locks stall some tenants and not others, a failure mid-fleet leaves split state, and per-tenant data-shape differences (one tenant's giant table) break timing assumptions.
Make every migration idempotent and resumable, alert on stuck tenants, and never hand-patch a single tenant outside the pipeline.
layman: Renovating 5,000 apartments in one tower: you go floor by floor with tenants still living there, keep old and new plumbing working during the switch, and track exactly which floors are done.
followups: What does expand-and-contract mean in this context?
How does application code know a tenant's schema version?
What happens when tenant 3,201 fails mid-migration?

redflags: Runs one script across all schemas in a single transaction
memory: Fleet rollout: version per tenant, canary first, expand-and-contract, idempotent and resumable.

title: Multi-Tenant RAG and Vector Store Isolation
question: Each customer uploads their own private documents into an AI assistant. How do you keep them apart in the vector store, and what leaks if you get it wrong?
technical: Pick the isolation level like any tenancy decision: shared index with a mandatory tenant filter (cheapest, riskiest), namespace or collection per tenant (middle), or dedicated index for regulated customers.
Enforce the tenant filter server-side in one retrieval gateway — never trust the calling service or the prompt to include it.
Apply document-level ACLs on top of tenant isolation: within a tenant, a user must not retrieve HR documents they cannot open.

Failure modes: a missing filter silently returns cross-tenant chunks the model then quotes, one tenant's bulk re-index degrades everyone's retrieval latency, and deleted documents live on in the index when deletion never reaches the vectors.
Test isolation continuously: plant synthetic canary documents per tenant and run automated cross-tenant retrieval probes that must return nothing.
layman: A shared law-firm archive where every folder is stamped with the client's name and the archivist physically cannot hand you another client's folder — even if you ask nicely.
code:
def retrieve(tenant_id, user, query):
    hits = index.search(
        embed(query), top_k=20,
        filter={"tenant_id": tenant_id})   # enforced server-side, always
    return [h for h in hits if acl.allows(user, h.doc_id)][:8]
followups: Shared index or per-tenant index — what are the decision criteria?
How is document deletion propagated to the vectors?
How would you detect a cross-tenant leak in production?
When would a tenant need its own embedding model?

Claims embeddings are anonymous so leakage is harmless

title: Tenant Tiers with Different SLOs and Isolation
question: Product wants Free, Pro and Enterprise tiers with different limits and uptime promises. How do you build that without ending up maintaining three products?
technical: One codebase, tier as configuration: quotas, feature flags, SLOs and isolation level are tenant metadata, not separate deployments.
Map tiers to isolation levels: pooled infrastructure for Free and Pro, dedicated node pools or database instances for Enterprise.
Give tiers separate capacity pools and error budgets so a Free-tier surge cannot burn the Enterprise SLO.

Known issues: tier upgrades become data migrations (pooled to dedicated), per-tier SLOs need per-tier SLIs because a global dashboard hides an Enterprise-only outage, and one-off Enterprise customisations quietly fork the platform unless resisted.
Price against real infrastructure cost: dedicated isolation is expensive, and tiering that ignores it destroys margins.
layman: Economy, business and first class fly on the same plane: same pilots and engine, but different seats, service and boarding — and the airline still tracks punctuality per cabin.

What exactly happens during a pooled-to-dedicated upgrade?

title: Per-Tenant Data Residency
question: New enterprise customers say their data must stay in the EU or in Singapore. How do you add that to a platform that never thought about regions, and what breaks?
technical: Split the system into control plane (tenant registry, billing — global metadata) and data plane (documents, records — region-pinned per tenant).
Route at the edge: a thin global router looks up the tenant's home region and forwards; tenant content never leaves its region.
Backups, DR, logs, caches, queues and search indexes must all respect the pin — one document body in a global log sink already violates residency.

What breaks: global features (cross-region search, analytics, shared model fine-tuning) must be rebuilt per region or fed only non-content signals, and DR must fail over within the approved region set, which weakens naive multi-region designs.
Prove it with a data-flow inventory and automated residency tests per subsystem — auditors ask where every copy lives, including the transient ones.
layman: Some clients require their files to stay in the Singapore office. Reception can tell you which office a client belongs to, but the files never get couriered abroad — including the photocopies and the shredding bin.

region = registry.home_region(tenant_id)   # global control plane
if region != CURRENT_REGION:
    return proxy_to(region, request)       # content stays in-region
handle_locally(request)                    # incl. logs and backups

Global log or analytics sinks receive tenant content

title: Multi-Tenant Caching
question: How do you cache in a shared system so that no customer ever sees another's data, and one busy customer cannot push everyone else out of the cache?
technical: Tenant ID is part of every cache key, added centrally by one cache client library — never left to individual call sites to remember.
Guard the two classic failures: key collisions leak data across tenants, and a shared LRU lets one big tenant evict everyone else's entries — the in-memory noisy neighbour.
Bound per-tenant capacity: per-tenant key budgets, partitioned caches, or separate pools for heavy tiers.
Invalidate per tenant: offboarding and permission changes must clear exactly that tenant's entries — a versioned namespace per tenant makes this one counter bump.
Never share cached content that embeds authorisation: a rendered response cached for tenant A and served to tenant B is a breach, not a bug. The same applies to shared LLM response caches.
layman: Hotel room safes: every guest's safe opens only with their own code, each room has its own safe rather than one shared locker, and checkout wipes that room's safe — not the whole hotel's.

What stops one tenant filling the entire cache?

How would you detect a cross-tenant cache hit?

One shared LRU with no per-tenant bounds
Offboarding leaves tenant data in cache

title: Storing User Passwords Safely
question: How do you store user passwords? Why is encrypting them the wrong answer?
technical: Encryption is reversible by design, so it only moves the problem to the key — anyone holding the database and the key holds every password. Password storage is a one-way problem: hash, never encrypt, and never store plaintext.

General-purpose hashes are the wrong tool for the opposite reason: MD5 and SHA-256 are built to be fast, and commodity GPUs try them in the billions per second. Use a deliberately expensive password KDF — Argon2id first choice, scrypt or bcrypt otherwise, PBKDF2 where FIPS compliance forces it.

Tune cost to your hardware, not to a blog post: OWASP's baseline is Argon2id at 19 MiB, 2 iterations, parallelism 1, or bcrypt cost 10–12 — then measure and aim for roughly 100–250 ms per verification on production hardware. Argon2 and scrypt are also memory-hard, which is what actually blunts GPU and ASIC attacks.

A unique random salt per user kills rainbow tables and stops identical passwords producing identical hashes; bcrypt and Argon2 generate and embed it in the output string, so you store one field, not two. A pepper — HMAC-SHA256(password, key) with the key in a KMS or HSM, never in the database — means a stolen database alone is not enough, and the key can be rotated.

Verify by recomputing and comparing in constant time, then rehash transparently on successful login when parameters have moved on. Around it: throttle per account and per IP, return the same message for wrong user and wrong password, screen against known-breached passwords, allow long passphrases, and prefer progressive delays over permanent lockout, which is itself a denial-of-service lever.
layman: You do not keep a copy of the key to someone's house so you can check it later. You keep the shape of the lock it turns — and you make testing each candidate key slow enough that trying millions is pointless.
usecases: Rotating a legacy MD5 or SHA-1 password table
Service and API credentials at rest
code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError
import hmac, hashlib, os

PEPPER = os.environ["PASSWORD_PEPPER"].encode()      # from KMS, not the DB
ph = PasswordHasher(memory_cost=19456, time_cost=2, parallelism=1)

def pre(password: str) -> bytes:                     # pepper before hashing
    return hmac.new(PEPPER, password.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()

def store(password: str) -> str:
    return ph.hash(pre(password))                    # salt is generated + embedded

def verify(stored: str, password: str) -> bool:
    try:
        ph.verify(stored, pre(password))             # constant-time inside
    except VerifyMismatchError:
        return False
    if ph.check_needs_rehash(stored):                # upgrade cost silently
        save(ph.hash(pre(password)))
    return True
followups: Your table is full of unsalted MD5 hashes. How do you migrate without a forced reset?
Where does the pepper live, and how do you rotate it?

Login is now 200 ms of CPU per attempt. How do you stop that becoming the DoS vector?
redflags: Says encrypt, or reversible so we can email it back
Uses MD5, SHA-1 or plain SHA-256, or writes their own hashing scheme
One shared salt for every user, or a salt kept alongside a hash with no per-user randomness
Caps password length at 12 characters, or strips characters before hashing
Compares hashes with == and has no rate limiting on the login endpoint
memory: Argon2id, unique salt, KMS pepper, slow by design — plus rate limiting; encryption is reversible, so never.

title: Common Web Application Security Risks
question: Which security holes keep showing up in web applications, and what stops each one?
technical: Broken access control and IDOR (guessing or editing an ID in a request to reach another user's data), injection, XSS (a malicious script that runs inside another user's browser), CSRF (tricking a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request they never intended), authentication failure, SSRF (tricking the server itself into calling internal systems on the attacker's behalf), insecure configuration, vulnerable dependencies and data exposure.
Use server-side authorisation, parameterised queries, output encoding, CSP, secure sessions, egress control, scanning and logging.
Threat-model the actual system instead of only reciting names.
layman: Attackers look for unlocked doors, forged forms, unsafe links and trusted staff who accept unverified instructions.
usecases: Prevent cross-tenant invoice access and SSRF in URL-fetch features.
code:
Interview focus:
- Security knowledge must connect threats to enforcement and testing.
followups: Which risk is most likely in this design?
How is it tested?
memory: Security knowledge must connect threats to enforcement and testing.

title: Secret Management
question: Where do passwords, API keys and certificates live, and how do you rotate them?
technical: Use Secret Manager or equivalent, not source control, images or ordinary configuration.
Prefer workload identity and short-lived credentials.
Apply least privilege, rotation, audit and environment separation.
Redact logs and revoke accidental exposure immediately.
layman: Keep keys in a guarded vault, not written on an office wall.
usecases: GKE workload obtains a database secret through Secret Manager.
code:
Interview focus:
- Use managed identity first and a dedicated vault for unavoidable secrets.
followups: How is rotation performed without outage?
What happens after a secret is committed?
memory: Use managed identity first and a dedicated vault for unavoidable secrets.

question: Your API is out on the internet. How do you stop people scraping it, spamming it or guessing their way in?
technical: Authenticate, authorise, validate input and limit request sizes.
Apply per-user or tenant quotas, rate and concurrency limits, timeouts, WAF or bot controls and replay or idempotency protection.
Monitor anomalies and add cost controls for expensive operations.
layman: A public service counter needs identity checks, queue limits, form validation and the ability to block abusive visitors.
usecases: Protect an AI endpoint from token-cost abuse.
code:
Interview focus:
- Protect API capacity, downstream systems and business cost.
followups: Where is rate limiting enforced?
How do service tiers differ?
memory: Protect API capacity, downstream systems and business cost.

question: Who gets admin access to production, and what has to be true every time they use it?
technical: Use separate privileged identities, MFA and least privilege.
Use just-in-time time-bound elevation, approval, audit and regular access review.
Avoid shared accounts and maintain a monitored break-glass process.
layman: Master keys are checked out temporarily, approved and recorded; they are not copied for everyone.
usecases: Temporary production database access during an incident.
code:
Interview focus:
- Privileged access should be temporary, approved, attributable and audited.
followups: How is break-glass tested?
Who reviews access?
memory: Privileged access should be temporary, approved, attributable and audited.

title: Logs, Metrics and Traces
question: Logs, metrics and traces. What does each one tell you, and when do you reach for which?
technical: Logs are detailed individual events.
Metrics are aggregated numeric measurements over time.
Traces follow one request across components.
Use all three with shared service, version and trace context.
layman: Logs are diary entries, metrics are dashboard gauges and traces are the route of one parcel through every station.
usecases: Investigate a slow payment across API, queue and provider.
code:
Interview focus:
- Logs explain events, metrics reveal patterns and traces show distributed flow.
followups: Which is best for alerting?
How are logs linked to traces?
memory: Logs explain events, metrics reveal patterns and traces show distributed flow.

title: What Should Be Logged
question: What belongs in a log, and what must never end up in one?
technical: Log timestamp, service and version, severity, trace ID, operation, result, duration and safe tenant context.
Do not log passwords, tokens, keys, full payment details or unnecessary personal and confidential data.
Use structured fields with retention and access controls.
layman: Write enough to reconstruct what happened, but never copy the safe’s contents into the incident diary.
code:
Interview focus:
- Logs must be useful, structured and safe.
followups: How is PII redacted?
How is high-volume logging sampled?
memory: Logs must be useful, structured and safe.

title: Actionable Alerts
question: What makes an alert worth waking someone up for?
technical: It indicates real or imminent user or business impact and requires human action.
It has severity, owner, context, dashboard and runbook links and avoids duplicates.
Alert on SLO burn, transaction failure or saturation rather than every exception.
layman: An alarm should mean someone must act, not merely that a sensor noticed one harmless event.
usecases: Payment failures exceed threshold for ten minutes.
code:
Interview focus:
- Actionable alerts are impact-based, owned and linked to a response.
followups: Who is paged?
What is the false-positive rate?
memory: Actionable alerts are impact-based, owned and linked to a response.

title: Post-Incident Review
question: The incident is over. What goes into the write-up, and what is the point of it?
technical: Impact, timeline, detection, root cause, contributing factors and recovery.
What worked and failed, with corrective actions, owners and due dates.
Focus on system learning rather than individual blame.
layman: After a fire, improve wiring, alarms and procedures instead of blaming the person nearest the switch.
code:
Interview focus:
- A review is complete only when learning becomes tracked system change.
followups: Root cause versus contributing factor?
How are actions tracked?
memory: A review is complete only when learning becomes tracked system change.

title: Production Testing Strategy
question: What mix of tests does a production system actually need?
technical: Use unit, component, integration, contract and targeted end-to-end tests.
Add security, performance, resilience, migration, smoke and synthetic production checks.
Balance confidence and execution speed; excessive end-to-end tests become slow and fragile.
layman: Test parts, important connections, complete customer journeys and failure conditions.
code:
Interview focus:
- A production test portfolio covers logic, integration, non-functional behaviour and deployment.
followups: What belongs in end-to-end testing?
How are third parties simulated?
memory: A production test portfolio covers logic, integration, non-functional behaviour and deployment.

title: Contract Testing
question: What is contract testing, and which problem between teams does it solve?
technical: It verifies that a service consumer and provider agree on request, response, fields, types and error behaviour.
It catches breaking integration changes without requiring a complete end-to-end environment.
layman: Both departments agree on the exact form and response before either changes its process.
usecases: Subscription service verifies its contract with payment service.
code:
Interview focus:
- Contract tests protect service compatibility at integration boundaries.
followups: Who owns the contract?
How are versions handled?
memory: Contract tests protect service compatibility at integration boundaries.

title: Testing Multi-Tenancy
question: How do you test that tenants really are isolated, instead of just hoping they are?
technical: Verify tenant A cannot read, update, delete, search, export or download tenant B data.
Test caches, signed URLs, jobs, admin roles, search indexes and audit.
Use identical-looking IDs or names across tenants to expose missing scoping.
layman: Try every door with the wrong company badge, including hidden service doors and archive rooms.
usecases: Automated negative tests for invoice and file access.
code:
Interview focus:
- Multi-tenancy testing must cover every storage and processing path with negative cases.
followups: How are async jobs tested?
How are platform admins separated?
memory: Multi-tenancy testing must cover every storage and processing path with negative cases.

title: Performance Testing
question: How do you find out how much load your system can take before your users find out for you?
technical: Define realistic journeys, traffic shapes, data volume and NFRs.
Test baseline, peak, stress and recovery with gradual ramp-up.
Measure p50, p95, p99, errors, throughput, saturation, dependencies and autoscaling.
Use production-like data and compare against explicit targets.
layman: Test the road during normal traffic, rush hour and beyond capacity, then confirm it recovers.
usecases: Load-test a Ramadan peak traffic profile.
code:
Interview focus:
- Performance testing validates percentiles, capacity, bottlenecks and recovery.
followups: What is the breaking point?
How is the database represented realistically?
memory: Performance testing validates percentiles, capacity, bottlenecks and recovery.

title: Software Project Estimation
question: How do you estimate a piece of work when you cannot yet see all of it?
technical: Decompose requirements and state assumptions, dependencies and unknowns.
Include NFRs, security, testing, migration, environments, CI/CD, documentation and support.
Use historical data and discovery or spikes for high uncertainty and expose ranges and contingency.
layman: Estimate permits, foundations, inspections and maintenance, not only construction time.
usecases: Estimate a cloud migration or AI-integration project.
code:
Interview focus:
- A credible estimate includes delivery, quality, operations and uncertainty.
followups: Which uncertainty dominates?
What is explicitly excluded?
memory: A credible estimate includes delivery, quality, operations and uncertainty.

title: Balance Delivery Speed and Quality
question: The business wants it faster and the team wants it done properly. How do you hold that balance?
technical: Set non-negotiable security and reliability controls and automate them.
Reduce scope or use controlled rollout rather than silently lowering quality.
Distinguish reversible decisions from hard-to-reverse decisions.
Accept technical debt only with explicit risk, owner and remediation plan.
layman: Deliver fewer safe features rather than a larger unsafe package.
usecases: Ship the core workflow behind feature flags and defer non-essential features.
code:
Interview focus:
- Balance speed through scope, automation and reversible delivery—not hidden risk.
followups: Which controls are non-negotiable?
How is debt recorded?
redflags: Quality always sacrificed for the date
memory: Balance speed through scope, automation and reversible delivery—not hidden risk.

title: Repeated Poor-Quality Delivery
question: One developer keeps shipping work that comes back broken. How do you handle it?
technical: Use concrete examples and determine whether the cause is skill, clarity, workload or motivation.
Set measurable expectations and provide pairing, training and review support.
Review progress and document persistent performance concerns; escalate appropriately if improvement does not occur.
layman: Diagnose whether the worker lacks training, tools or clarity before deciding the response.
usecases: Improve API error handling and testing over a defined period.
code:
Interview focus:
- Coach with evidence and expectations, then use the performance process if needed.
followups: What evidence is used?
How long is the improvement plan?
memory: Coach with evidence and expectations, then use the performance process if needed.

title: Avoid the Tech Lead Bottleneck
question: Everything on the team ends up waiting for you. How do you fix that?
technical: Delegate domain ownership and develop senior engineers.
Document principles and decisions and automate routine quality controls.
Use structured design reviews and clear escalation instead of reviewing every change.
Promote shared knowledge and rotate operational responsibility.
layman: The lead designs the system and develops supervisors; they do not personally inspect every screw forever.
usecases: Domain leads own identity, billing and data components.
code:
Interview focus:
- A Tech Lead scales through standards, automation and capable owners.
followups: Which decisions still require the Tech Lead?
How is consistency maintained?
memory: A Tech Lead scales through standards, automation and capable owners.

title: Engineering Effectiveness Metrics
question: How would you tell whether an engineering team is doing well, without counting lines of code?
technical: Use deployment frequency, change lead time, change-failure rate and MTTR.
Add escaped defects, SLO attainment, vulnerability age, PR cycle time, build reliability and cost per transaction.
Use team and system outcomes; avoid lines of code, commits and individual story points as productivity measures.
layman: Measure how reliably the factory delivers useful products, not how many hammer swings each worker makes.
usecases: DORA metrics plus reliability, security and cost indicators.
code:
Interview focus:
- Measure flow, quality, reliability, security and business outcomes.
followups: How can each metric be gamed?
Which business outcome does it support?
memory: Measure flow, quality, reliability, security and business outcomes.

title: Firestore versus PostgreSQL
question: Firestore or PostgreSQL for a real product? And how does that choice generalise to SQL versus NoSQL?
technical: Firestore is a managed document database with flexible schema, real-time listeners and query patterns that should be designed in advance.
PostgreSQL is relational and supports rich SQL, joins, constraints and strong ACID workflows.
Use PostgreSQL for payments, subscriptions and relational consistency; use Firestore for document-oriented real-time state when its access model fits.
Compare transactions, indexes, scale, tenant isolation, analytics and cost rather than saying one is faster.

In general, choose SQL for relational constraints, joins and transactions; choose NoSQL for specific document or key access patterns and horizontal scale, accepting denormalisation and application-enforced rules.
layman: Firestore is a flexible document cabinet; PostgreSQL is a structured ledger with enforced relationships and rules.
usecases: Subscriptions in PostgreSQL and flexible user preferences in Firestore.
code:
Interview focus:
- Choose from data relationships, consistency, query patterns and operational model.
followups: How is tenant isolation enforced?
How are ad-hoc reports handled?
Can both be used?
What is the most important query?
Which rule must the database enforce?
memory: Choose from data relationships, consistency, query patterns and operational model.

title: Large File Upload
question: Someone needs to upload a 20 GB file over a connection that keeps dropping. How do you make that work?
technical: Create an authorised upload session and issue a short-lived resumable or signed URL for direct object-storage upload.
Record tenant, expected metadata, quota, state and expiry and verify size, checksum, signature and content type.
Quarantine and malware-scan files and protect against archive or decompression bombs.
Trigger idempotent asynchronous processing and use lifecycle rules for abandoned uploads.
layman: The user sends the large parcel directly to the warehouse with a temporary authorised delivery ticket instead of carrying it through reception.
usecases: Large video, PDF archive or dataset upload to Cloud Storage.
code:
Interview focus:
- Large uploads should be direct, resumable, validated, quarantined and asynchronous.
followups: How is resume supported?
What if the completion event is duplicated?
How are orphan uploads cleaned?
redflags: Streams entire file through application server
memory: Large uploads should be direct, resumable, validated, quarantined and asynchronous.

title: Blue-Green Deployment
question: Explain blue-green deployment. What do you do about traffic, database changes, logged-in users, background workers, and rolling back?
technical: Maintain two production-capable environments: current blue and new green.
Deploy and validate green, then switch traffic while retaining blue for rapid reversal.
Use backward-compatible expand-and-contract database changes because both versions may share data.
Externalise sessions and prevent both versions from running duplicate scheduled or queue jobs.
Rollback may be unsafe after irreversible data changes.
layman: Prepare a second working shop, test it, redirect customers and keep the old shop ready until confidence is high.
usecases: Release a new API version with near-instant traffic reversal.
code:
Interview focus:
- Blue-green makes application rollback fast only when state remains compatible.
followups: How are WebSockets handled?
When is blue-green unsuitable?
How are duplicate workers prevented?
memory: Blue-green makes application rollback fast only when state remains compatible.

title: Scenario: Cross-Tenant Invoice Leak
question: A customer calls: for a moment, they saw another company's invoice. What do you do, and in what order?
technical: Declare a critical security incident and disable or isolate the affected path.
Preserve evidence, determine scope and revoke exposed links or sessions.
Engage security, privacy and legal processes and meet notification obligations.
Fix the isolation defect, search for similar paths, add tests and complete a security review.
layman: Treat confidential information delivered to the wrong customer as an emergency, not a normal bug.
code:
Interview focus:
- Contain, scope, notify, remediate and prevent recurrence.
followups: How is the affected population determined?
What evidence must be preserved?
memory: Contain, scope, notify, remediate and prevent recurrence.

title: Scenario: Latency Regression after Deployment
question: You deploy, and p95 latency jumps from 300 ms to eight seconds. What now?
technical: Confirm impact and correlate it with deployment timing.
Check error rate, saturation, traces, dependencies, database queries, connection pools and cache.
Roll back or disable the change when impact is material.
Verify recovery, reproduce the issue and add regression or performance controls.
layman: Return to the last safe version before spending a long time diagnosing while customers remain blocked.
usecases: A release introduces a table scan and pool exhaustion.
code:
Interview focus:
- Mitigate first, then diagnose and prevent the regression.
followups: What evidence justifies rollback?
How is complete recovery verified?
redflags: Keeps debugging for hours before mitigation
memory: Mitigate first, then diagnose and prevent the regression.

title: Scenario: Noisy Tenant Import
question: A large customer starts importing millions of records and everyone else's app slows to a crawl. What do you do?
technical: Throttle the tenant and separate interactive traffic from batch work.
Use asynchronous queueing, tenant quotas and concurrency limits and reserve capacity for critical paths.
Monitor cost and backlog and move exceptional tenants to dedicated infrastructure when justified.
layman: Move one customer’s bulk delivery to a separate loading bay so the main entrance remains usable.
code:
Interview focus:
- Protect fairness through workload separation and tenant-level controls.
followups: How is progress exposed?
What commercial tier applies?
memory: Protect fairness through workload separation and tenant-level controls.

title: Scenario: Partial Database Migration Failure
question: The deployment finished, but the database migration died halfway through. What do you do?
technical: Stop further rollout and inspect the exact migration state.
Do not blindly rerun; determine transactional boundaries and integrity.
Use resumable versioned migration, compatible application versions and roll-forward when rollback is unsafe.
Validate data and improve pre-deployment migration testing.
layman: Do not restart a half-completed construction job without checking which walls already moved.
usecases: A large backfill fails after partial completion.
code:
Interview focus:
- Partial migration recovery requires state inspection, compatibility and safe continuation.
followups: Was the migration transactional?
Can the old application read the new schema?
memory: Partial migration recovery requires state inspection, compatibility and safe continuation.

title: Scenario: Multi-Tenant Knowledge Assistant
question: Design a knowledge assistant for 100 organisations and 50,000 users, with citations, an audit trail and 99.9% uptime.
technical: Cover requirements, ingestion, OCR and parsing, chunking, retrieval, ACLs, generation, security, reliability, LLMOps, operations and cost.
Handle malicious documents, model latency, embedding reindexing, deletion, cross-tenant leaks, cost increases and queue backlog.
Show failure boundaries, metrics and recovery.
layman: Design the intelligent librarian, locked archives, audit desk, emergency procedures and budget controls.
code:
Interview focus:
- A lead-level design includes failures, governance, operations and cost.
followups: Where is authorisation enforced?
How is reindexing performed without downtime?
memory: A lead-level design includes failures, governance, operations and cost.

title: Scenario: Production-Readiness Code Review
question: Review this queue consumer: it acknowledges messages before doing the work, retries forever, has no timeouts, keeps secrets in config and barely logs anything. What do you flag, and in what order?
technical: Group findings under correctness, reliability, security, operability, scalability, consistency, deployment and testing.
Prioritise early acknowledgement, duplicate side effects, secret exposure and unbounded failure amplification.
Add durable idempotency, transactional state or outbox, bounded retries and DLQ, timeouts, backpressure, graceful shutdown and observability.
layman: Review the machine by safety category and fix the faults most likely to harm customers first.
usecases: Node.js or Python Pub/Sub consumer review exercise.
code:
Interview focus:
- Lead-level review prioritises business correctness and failure containment.
followups: Which issue has the highest blast radius?
What must be fixed before production?
redflags: Lists code style before correctness and security
memory: Lead-level review prioritises business correctness and failure containment.

title: Bias–Variance Trade-off
question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff? Explain how it turns up as underfitting and overfitting, and what you do about it in practice.
technical: Bias is systematic error from an overly simple model; variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample.
High bias appears as underfitting: both training and validation performance are poor. High variance appears as overfitting: training performance is strong but validation performance degrades.
Manage bias with richer features/models and better optimisation. Manage variance with more data, regularisation, simpler models, pruning, dropout, ensembling and cross-validation.
Choose the operating point using validation performance and business cost, not training accuracy alone.
layman: A model can be too rigid to learn the pattern or so flexible that it memorises every training example.
usecases: Selecting model complexity for fraud detection
Choosing tree depth or regularisation strength
code:
Example:
A shallow tree misses fraud patterns (high bias).
A fully grown tree memorises training cases (high variance).
Cross-validation helps select a middle depth.
followups: How would learning curves reveal bias or variance?
Why can bagging reduce variance?
redflags: Uses the test set repeatedly for tuning
memory: Underfit = high bias; overfit = high variance; validation data finds the balance.

title: Bayes' Theorem
question: State Bayes' theorem and walk through a real example, such as a spam filter or a medical test that comes back positive.
technical: Bayes' theorem updates a prior belief after observing evidence: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
The prior is the base rate, the likelihood describes how probable the evidence is under the hypothesis, and the posterior is the updated probability.
Base rates matter: even a highly accurate test can produce many false positives when the condition is rare.
layman: Start with what was likely before the evidence, then update it according to how strongly the evidence supports each possibility.
usecases: Fraud risk after a suspicious event
code:
Medical example:
Prevalence = 1%, sensitivity = 99%, false-positive rate = 5%.
Among 10,000 people: about 99 true positives and 495 false positives.
A positive result therefore does not mean a 99% chance of disease.
followups: What is the base-rate fallacy?
How does Naive Bayes use the theorem?
redflags: Says test accuracy equals posterior probability
memory: Posterior = prior updated by evidence; never ignore the base rate.

title: Probability vs. Likelihood
question: What is the difference between probability and likelihood?
technical: Probability treats model parameters as fixed and asks how probable different data outcomes are.
Likelihood treats observed data as fixed and compares how well different parameter values explain it.
The same mathematical expression can be read differently depending on what is considered variable. Maximum-likelihood estimation chooses parameters that maximise the observed-data likelihood.
layman: Probability asks, “Given this coin, what data might I see?” Likelihood asks, “Given these flips, which coin bias best explains them?”
code:
Example:
P(7 heads | p=0.6) is a probability of data.
L(p | 7 heads, 3 tails) is a function comparing candidate values of p.
followups: Is likelihood a probability distribution over parameters?
How does maximum likelihood relate to cross-entropy?
redflags: Says they are identical without explaining the viewpoint
Assumes likelihood must sum to one over parameters
memory: Probability varies data; likelihood varies parameters for fixed observed data.

title: P-values and Statistical Significance
question: What does a p-value actually tell you? And what do people wrongly assume when they see one below 0.05?
technical: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and model assumptions are true, of observing a result at least as extreme as the one obtained.
p < 0.05 does not mean there is a 95% probability the alternative is true, nor that the effect is large or practically important.
