Version every input that can move the result: prompt, model, retrieval settings, tool definitions. If an experiment cannot tell you which of those changed, it cannot tell you what caused the drop.

Close the loop in production. Online evaluators scoring a sample of live traffic turn drift into a chart you watch rather than a support ticket you receive, and they catch the failures your dataset never imagined.
layman: Changing a recipe to please one diner. You cook the same ten dishes again and check nobody else's dinner got worse.
code:
from langsmith import Client, evaluate
client = Client()

# grow the dataset from real traces, especially the bad ones
runs = client.list_runs(project_name="support-agent-prod",
                        filter='and(eq(feedback_key,"user_score"), lt(feedback_score,1))',
                        limit=50)
client.create_examples(dataset_name="support-golden-v4",
                       inputs=[r.inputs for r in runs],
                       outputs=[{"expected": review(r)} for r in runs])

def grounded(run, example):
    cited = set(run.outputs["chunk_ids"])
    return {"key": "grounded", "score": float(cited <= set(run.outputs["retrieved"]))}

exp = evaluate(target, data="support-golden-v4",
               evaluators=[grounded, correct_tool_called, judge_helpfulness],
               experiment_prefix=f"prompt-{PROMPT_V}",
               metadata={"model": MODEL, "prompt_version": PROMPT_V})
# CI fails when any metric drops more than the threshold vs the last experiment
followups: How many examples are enough, and what makes a bad one?
How do you keep the dataset honest as the product changes?
Would you block a release on a judge score alone? Why not?
Who signs off a prompt change, and what do they look at?
redflags: Compares two prompts by eye and ships
Looks only at the average score
Uses a judge that was never calibrated
Dataset written by the same person who wrote the prompt
memory: Curate cases from real traces, compare experiments per example, and calibrate the judge before it gates a release.

title: From a Thumbs-Down to a Fixed Prompt
question: A user clicks thumbs-down on an answer. Walk me through everything that has to be wired up for that click to become a fix.
technical: The run must be identifiable at the moment you answer. Capture the run or trace id while generating and return it to the client, so feedback attaches to that exact run instead of to a timestamp somebody has to correlate by hand.

The feedback is written back against the run, and the trace carries the context that explains it: retrieved chunks, tool calls, model version, prompt version. Without that link you know something was wrong but never what.

Triage needs to be automatic. A rule routes negative-feedback runs into an annotation queue where a human labels the actual failure: wrong retrieval, wrong tool, right facts with the wrong tone, or a user disagreeing with a correct answer.

The label decides where the fix goes, and they are different places: retrieval into the index or chunking, tool problems into the tool contract, tone into the prompt. Every confirmed case is added to the dataset so the fix stays fixed.

Read the aggregate rather than the anecdote. Feedback rate by tenant, by version and over time tells you whether you are improving; a single thumbs-down is a story, and a meaningful share of them are users disagreeing with an answer that was right.
layman: A complaint card that arrives with the receipt attached. Without the receipt you know someone was unhappy, but not what they ordered.
usecases: Support escalation from an AI answer
Building a dataset from real failures
followups: The user gives feedback ten minutes later from another page. Does it still attach?
How do you handle feedback that is simply wrong?
Who reads the annotation queue, and how often?
How long is the loop from complaint to a released fix?
redflags: Stores thumbs in its own table with no link to the run
Nobody is responsible for reading it
Treats every complaint as a defect
memory: Return the run id with the answer. Feedback that cannot find its run is just a number on a dashboard.

title: Living With LangChain Upgrades
question: You are a year behind on LangChain and every upgrade breaks something. How do you keep a production application on a framework that moves this fast?
technical: Pin exact versions and upgrade on purpose. The core package, the umbrella package and each provider integration move on their own cadence, and core is what decides compatibility, so a lockfile plus a scheduled upgrade slot beats an emergency bump during an incident.

Keep the framework at the edges. A thin internal interface, your own function that takes a question and returns an answer, means a breaking change touches a handful of files rather than the whole codebase, and lets you drop the abstraction on one path without a rewrite.

Know what you are buying. The value is provider-agnostic messages and tool calls, the integration surface and the ecosystem around it. If your application is one prompt against one provider, the vendor SDK is less code and one fewer dependency to chase.

Migrations follow a rhythm: the old API keeps working, gets deprecated, then goes. Agent executors giving way to the newer agent constructor, Pydantic v1 to v2, providers moving out of the monolith into their own packages. Move at the deprecation warning, not at the removal.

Your evaluation dataset is the real upgrade test. Code that type-checks can still behave differently because prompt formatting, message coercion and tool-call handling change between versions, so run the experiment before and after every bump.
layman: Renovating with a supplier who keeps changing their fittings. You keep the plumbing behind one panel so next year's change is a panel, not the whole house.
usecases: Regulated environments with slow dependency approval
Deciding whether to keep or drop the framework
code:
# pin the pieces that move independently
langchain-core==<pinned>
langchain==<pinned>
langchain-openai==<pinned>
langgraph==<pinned>

# keep the framework behind one seam
class AnswerService:
    """Everything LangChain-shaped lives below this line."""
    def answer(self, question: str, ctx: Context) -> Answer:
        result = self._graph.invoke(...)
        return Answer(text=..., citations=..., usage=...)

# upgrade procedure: bump -> run the same eval dataset -> compare experiments
# a green test suite is not evidence that behaviour is unchanged
followups: When would you drop the framework entirely for a given path?
How do you test an upgrade beyond the test suite?
Which kinds of change break quietly rather than loudly?
Who owns dependency upgrades on your team?
redflags: Framework calls scattered through business logic
Upgrades postponed until something forces it
Ships an upgrade without re-running evaluations
memory: Pin it, wrap it behind one seam, upgrade on a schedule, and re-run the evals because behaviour moves even when code compiles.

title: Structured Output That Survives Production
question: Structured output works perfectly on your laptop and fails a few times an hour in production. What is actually going wrong, and what do you do about it?
technical: Underneath it is either tool calling or a constrained JSON mode, and providers differ in how strictly they enforce a schema. Failures cluster in predictable places: unusual inputs, refusals, output truncated by the token limit, and streaming, none of which appear in a happy-path demo.

Design the schema for the model as well as the database. Shallow beats deeply nested, enums beat free text, field descriptions carry the instruction, and every optional field needs an explicit unknown value or the model invents something plausible to fill it.

Handle failure as a normal path: keep the raw response so you can see what came back, retry once with the validation error fed back in, then fall back to a simpler schema or a safe default. A validation exception surfaced to the user is not error handling.

Structure is not truth. A perfectly typed object can be entirely wrong, so validate the values against your own systems before acting on them: does that order id exist, is that amount within policy, is that date in the future.
Track the validation failure rate per model version as a metric with an alert on it. Provider-side changes show up as a step change in that rate days before anyone raises a support ticket.
layman: Asking someone to fill in a form. Give them a short form with tick boxes and you get usable answers; give them a long one with blank boxes and they will write something in every field, whether they know it or not.
usecases: Anything whose output another system consumes
code:
class Extraction(BaseModel):
    intent: Literal["refund", "status", "complaint", "other"]     # enum, not free text
    order_id: str | None = Field(None, description="Format ORD-12345, null if absent")
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)

chain = model.with_structured_output(Extraction, include_raw=True)

def extract(text: str) -> Extraction:
    out = chain.invoke(text)
    if out["parsing_error"]:
        out = chain.invoke(f"{text}\n\nYour last reply failed validation: "
                           f"{out['parsing_error']}. Return valid JSON only.")
    if out["parsing_error"]:
        metrics.incr("extraction.failed", tags=[f"model:{MODEL}"])
        return Extraction(intent="other", confidence=0.0)          # safe default
    parsed = out["parsed"]
    if parsed.order_id and not orders.exists(parsed.order_id):     # shape is not truth
        parsed.order_id = None
    return parsed
followups: The model refuses instead of returning the object. What happens next?
How do you stream a structured response to a UI?
The provider you need does not support tool calling. Now what?
How do you version a schema that another team already consumes?
redflags: Deeply nested schema with free-text fields
Trusts values because the object validated
Falls back to regex over free text
memory: Shallow schema, keep the raw reply, retry once with the error, fall back safely, and validate values as well as shape.

title: Taking a Langflow Flow to Production
question: A team built a working assistant on the Langflow canvas and the business now wants it live for real customers. What has to change before that is a good idea?
technical: The defaults are prototype defaults: an embedded file-based database, automatic login rather than real authentication, and secrets typed into components on the canvas. Production needs an external Postgres, authentication and API keys turned on, and secrets in encrypted variables backed by a stable secret key, because rotating that key invalidates everything stored with it.

Flows are JSON artefacts, so treat them as build artefacts: exported into git, promoted from dev to staging to production through the API rather than rebuilt by hand in each environment. Reviewing a diff of flow JSON is genuinely painful, which is an argument for small flows with the real logic inside custom components.

Decide what the flow actually is. Serving internal tools and pilots from the visual runtime is reasonable; for a customer-facing path that needs retries, rate limiting, streaming, human-in-the-loop and tests, the flow is a design document you implement in code, and LangGraph is the natural target.

Operationally it is a web service with a database, so it needs the same things as any other: replicas behind a load balancer, health checks, resource limits, backups of the flow database, and an answer for flows that run longer than an HTTP request will wait.

Observability is not automatic. Point it at your tracing stack so a flow run produces the same traces as everything else, and put the same token budgets and rate limits in front of it that you would put in front of any other consumer of a paid model.
layman: A kitchen drawn on a design tool is not a kitchen. The drawing is genuinely useful, but nobody plumbs in the sink by printing the picture and hanging it on the wall.
usecases: Deciding whether to promote or rewrite
code:
# production configuration, not the quickstart
LANGFLOW_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/langflow
LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false
LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER=admin
LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY=<stable key from the secret manager; rotating breaks variables>
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=langflow-prod

# promote the same artefact rather than rebuilding by hand
# git: flows/support-assistant.json  (reviewed, tagged, deployed)
# POST /api/v1/flows/upload  with the exported JSON
# POST /api/v1/run/{flow_id}  with x-api-key
followups: How do you code-review a change to a flow?
Who is allowed to edit the production flow, and when?
The pod restarts and the flow database was local. What just happened?
What is the signal that this flow should be rewritten in code?
redflags: File-based database on a pod with no persistent volume
Secrets typed into components on the canvas
memory: External database, real authentication, encrypted secrets, flow JSON in git, and be clear whether the flow is the product or the blueprint.

title: Flow Governance When Analysts Build
question: Your Langflow canvas is now edited by analysts rather than engineers. How do you let them build without letting them ship something unsafe?
technical: Put the risky logic inside custom components rather than on the canvas. A component is Python you own, reviewed and tested, holding the tool contract, timeouts, retries and permission checks. Analysts compose components; they do not hand-write the part that can spend money or delete rows.

Separate environments and permissions. Building happens on a development instance, production runs a promoted flow that nobody edits live, and the ability to publish is a role rather than a default. Without that, a Tuesday afternoon experiment becomes a customer incident.

Offer a paved path: a library of approved components, your retriever, your model wrapper with rate limiting already inside it, your sanctioned tools. When the default way to build is also the safe way, unapproved components become the exception that gets reviewed rather than the norm.

A flow change is a behaviour change, so the same rules apply as to code: run it against the evaluation dataset before promotion and trace it afterwards. Otherwise you have a system whose behaviour is edited by people with no way of knowing whether they made it worse.

Be honest about the ceiling. Branching, loops, retries, streaming and human-in-the-loop all get awkward on a canvas, and a flow sprouting conditional edges and error paths is telling you it has outgrown the tool. The canvas has already done its real job as a prototyping and communication surface.
layman: Give people a set of tested, pre-wired appliances they can arrange however they like. Do not hand them the fuse box and hope.
usecases: Analyst or operations teams building their own flows
Internal AI tooling at low engineering cost
Standardising retrieval and model access across a company
Deciding when to graduate a flow into code
code:
from langflow.custom import Component
from langflow.io import MessageTextInput, Output

class ApprovedRefundLookup(Component):
    """Reviewed, tested, permission-checked. The analyst just drops it on the canvas."""
    display_name = "Refund Lookup (approved)"
    inputs = [MessageTextInput(name="order_id", display_name="Order ID")]
    outputs = [Output(name="result", display_name="Result", method="run")]

    def run(self) -> str:
        if not self.user_can("refunds:read"):          # permission inside the component
            return "Not permitted for this user."
        try:
            order = orders.get(self.order_id, timeout=5)   # timeout inside, not on canvas
        except NotFound:
            return "No order with that id. Ask the customer to confirm it."
        return summarise(order)                        # short, structured, model-friendly
followups: An analyst needs a component that does not exist yet. What is the path?
How do you stop a flow quietly calling an expensive model on every request?
What do you do when two people edit the same flow?
What would make you move this flow into LangGraph?
redflags: Anyone with the URL can edit production
Tools and credentials wired ad hoc on the canvas
No evaluation before a flow is promoted
Growing conditional logic on a canvas instead of moving to code
memory: Analysts compose, engineers own the components: promote flows like code and evaluate before they go live.

title: CrewAI Crews Under Production Load
question: A CrewAI demo with four role-playing agents impressed everyone, and in production it is slow, expensive and gives a different answer every time. What is actually going wrong?
technical: Crews are built on role-play: each agent has a role, goal and backstory, and the model decides how much to say and when it is finished. That freedom is what makes the demo charming and the production system non-deterministic, so expected_output on every task, and structured output via output_pydantic, is what turns prose into something a downstream system can consume.

Cost comes from conversation. The hierarchical process adds a manager model on top of every delegation, and allow_delegation lets agents bounce work between themselves. Start sequential, turn delegation on only where it earns its keep, and cap the damage with max_iter, max_rpm and a request-level token budget.

Memory is not free or portable. Enabling crew memory writes embeddings and history to a local storage directory, which quietly means an ephemeral container loses it on restart and two replicas do not share it. Point the storage at a real volume or an external store, and know what is in it before promising a retention policy.

Failure handling is the weak spot. A task that throws takes the run with it, and long crews run for minutes, so treat a kickoff as a background job with a queue, a timeout, retries at the task boundary and idempotent tools, rather than something a web request waits on.

Test it like a pipeline, not like a chat. Pin the model version, evaluate against a dataset of real inputs, assert on the structured fields rather than the prose, and watch tokens per kickoff as a metric, because the failure mode is usually gradual cost drift rather than a crash.
layman: A meeting of enthusiastic colleagues will eventually produce a good answer, but the length of the meeting is not fixed and everyone is billing by the minute.
usecases: Rapid prototyping of a multi-role process
code:
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Brief(BaseModel):            # structure beats prose downstream
    summary: str
    risks: list[str]
    sources: list[str]

analyst = Agent(role="Market analyst", goal="Find and verify facts",
                backstory="Careful, cites sources.", tools=[search],
                allow_delegation=False,          # delegation is opt-in, not default
                max_iter=6, llm=MODEL)

task = Task(description="Research {company} funding history",
            expected_output="Three verified facts with sources",   # anti-rambling
            agent=analyst, output_pydantic=Brief)

crew = Crew(agents=[analyst, writer], tasks=[task, write_task],
            process=Process.sequential,          # hierarchical adds a manager LLM
            memory=True, max_rpm=60, verbose=False)

# run it as a job, not inside a request
result = crew.kickoff(inputs={"company": name})   # minutes, not milliseconds
# CREWAI_STORAGE_DIR=/data/crewai   <- otherwise memory dies with the container
followups: When would you use the hierarchical process, and what does it cost?
A task in the middle of the crew fails. What happens to the work already done?
Where does crew memory live by default, and what breaks when you scale to three replicas?
How would you make the output of a crew safe for another system to consume?
redflags: Runs a crew inside an HTTP request
Enables memory without knowing where it is stored
No token budget or cost monitoring per kickoff
memory: Constrain the role-play: structured outputs, delegation off by default, iteration and rate caps, and run kickoffs as background jobs.

title: CrewAI Flows: Putting Determinism Back In
question: Most of your process is fixed business logic with two genuinely fuzzy steps, but you built it all as autonomous agents. How do you restructure it in CrewAI?
technical: Flows are the deterministic layer: @start, @listen and @router give you an explicit event-driven graph with typed state you control, and a crew becomes one step inside it rather than the whole design. The rule of thumb is that anything you can express as an if-statement should be an if-statement.

State is a Pydantic model on the flow, so it is inspectable and testable, and @persist writes it so a flow can be resumed rather than restarted. Without persistence a crash in step seven means paying for steps one to six again.

Routing decisions belong in code wherever the input allows it. Use a router on a classified field rather than asking an agent to decide who acts next, which removes an entire class of non-determinism and a model call from every run.

Keep the agentic part small and bounded: one crew, a clear task, structured output, its own budget. That way the unpredictable part of the system has a fence around it and the rest can be tested like ordinary software.

Instrument the seams. Log the state transition at each listener, emit the structured output of each crew, and record tokens per step, so when quality drops you know which step moved rather than re-reading a transcript.
layman: A production line with one skilled craftsman at a single station beats a workshop where everyone wanders around deciding what to do next.
usecases: Business processes with a few judgement calls
Reducing cost of an over-agentic prototype
followups: Which parts of your process genuinely need an agent, and how did you decide?
What does @persist store, and where would you put it in production?
How do you test a flow without calling a model?
How is this different from what LangGraph gives you?
redflags: Uses agents for decisions a rule could make
No persisted state, so failures restart from scratch
Routing decided by an LLM on every run
Cannot say which step caused a quality drop
memory: Flows for the deterministic skeleton, crews for the genuinely fuzzy steps, and persisted state so a crash resumes.

title: Google ADK: Sessions, State and Memory in Production
question: Your ADK agent works perfectly in local development and forgets everything the moment you deploy two replicas. What did you miss, and how do sessions, state and memory actually differ?
technical: The default in-memory session service is a development convenience: it lives in one process, so a restart wipes it and a second replica cannot see it. Production means a database-backed session service or the managed Vertex service, chosen before launch rather than after the first support ticket.

Three different things get confused. Session is the current conversation and its events; state is the key-value scratchpad attached to it; memory is the searchable long-term store across sessions. Wanting the agent to remember last week is a memory service question, not a session one.

State prefixes carry real semantics: unprefixed keys are session-scoped, user: spans that user's sessions, app: is global, and temp: is not persisted at all. Getting these wrong is how one user's preference leaks into another's conversation in a multi-tenant deployment.

State should be written through the event flow, using an agent's output key or an explicit state delta, rather than mutated directly on a session object. Direct mutation is invisible to the runner, so it is not persisted, not replayed, and not visible in the trace.

Artifacts are separate again: files and binary data belong in the artifact service backed by object storage, not stuffed into state, or every session load starts dragging PDFs and images across the wire.
layman: The conversation you are having, the notepad next to you, and the filing cabinet behind you are three different things. Development mode keeps all three in your head and forgets them when you stand up.
usecases: Multi-turn assistants on Cloud Run or GKE
Agents that must recall earlier conversations
Handling uploaded files in an agent

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import DatabaseSessionService      # not InMemory in prod
from google.adk.memory import VertexAiMemoryBankService
from google.adk.artifacts import GcsArtifactService

agent = LlmAgent(name="support", model=MODEL,
                 instruction="Help with orders. Preferences: {user:language}",
                 tools=[lookup_order], output_key="last_answer")   # writes to state

runner = Runner(app_name="support", agent=agent,
                session_service=DatabaseSessionService(db_url=DB_URL),
                memory_service=VertexAiMemoryBankService(...),
                artifact_service=GcsArtifactService(bucket=BUCKET))

async for event in runner.run_async(user_id=uid, session_id=sid, new_message=msg):
    if event.is_final_response():
        yield event.content

# state scoping matters in multi-tenant systems:
#   "cart_items"      -> this session only
#   "user:language"   -> all sessions for this user
#   "app:model_flags" -> everyone
#   "temp:raw_tool"   -> never persisted

How does a preference get from one conversation into the next?
Where do uploaded files go, and why not into state?
How do you keep tenant A's state away from tenant B?

No thought about state key scoping in multi-tenant apps

title: Google ADK: Callbacks as the Control Plane
question: Security asks you to block certain tool calls, redact data before it reaches the model, and prove the agent behaves the same after every change. Where does that go in an ADK agent?
technical: Callbacks are the seam for all of it. Before and after hooks around the agent, the model and each tool let you inspect and, crucially, short-circuit: returning a response from a before-model or before-tool callback stops the call from ever happening, which is how you implement a real block rather than a polite instruction in the prompt.

Put policy in a callback, not in the instruction text. A before-tool callback checks permissions and argument sanity for the current user, a before-model callback redacts identifiers, an after-model callback screens the output. Prompt instructions are advisory, callbacks are enforced.

The same hooks carry observability and cost control: attach request and tenant identifiers, count tokens per step, cache expensive tool results, and enforce a per-run budget by refusing further model calls once it is spent.

Behaviour gets locked in with evaluation sets rather than assertions, scoring both the final response and the tool trajectory, since an agent that reaches the right answer through the wrong tools is a bug waiting to bite. Run them in CI with the model version pinned.

Compose deterministic structure with workflow agents where the process is known: sequential, parallel and loop agents make the shape explicit instead of hoping the model orchestrates itself, and each sub-agent stays small enough to evaluate on its own.
layman: A doorman who can actually stop someone entering is a different thing from a sign asking people not to come in. Callbacks are the doorman.
usecases: Redacting sensitive data before it reaches the model
Regression testing agent behaviour in CI
followups: Which callback do you use to stop a tool call, and what do you return?
Why is a permission check in the prompt not a control?
What does tool trajectory scoring catch that response scoring misses?
When would you reach for a sequential or loop agent instead of one LLM agent?
redflags: Enforces permissions by asking the model nicely
No way to block a tool call at runtime
One large agent where the process is actually fixed
memory: Callbacks are where policy, redaction, budgets and telemetry are enforced; evalsets are what keep behaviour from drifting.

title: OpenAI Agents SDK: Handoffs, Guardrails and Where Traces Go
question: You built an agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK. Legal asks where the conversation traces are stored, and the team asks why a jailbreak attempt still costs a full model call. What do you tell them?
technical: Tracing is on by default and goes to the provider's dashboard, which is a data-governance decision someone has to make consciously. Disable it or point the exporter at your own collector when prompts contain customer data, and record that decision somewhere auditable.

Input guardrails run alongside the agent and trip a tripwire that raises immediately, which is the point: a cheap classifier can stop an abusive or off-topic request before the expensive model call happens. Output guardrails do the same on the way back for leakage and policy.

Handoffs and agent-as-tool are different shapes. A handoff transfers control and the conversation continues in the other agent; agent-as-tool calls a sub-agent, gets a result and keeps control. Choosing wrongly is why some systems lose track of who is answering.

Bound the loop with a maximum number of turns and a timeout, then decide what happens when the ceiling is hit, because the default failure is an exception at the worst possible moment rather than a graceful partial answer.

Sessions give conversation history for free, but the default local storage is single-process; a real deployment needs a shared, durable session store and a retention policy, since that store now holds the full transcript.
layman: A bouncer who checks people at the door costs less than a waiter who takes an order, cooks the meal, and then throws it away.
usecases: Blocking abuse and off-topic use cheaply
code:
from agents import Agent, Runner, input_guardrail, GuardrailFunctionOutput
from agents import InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered, set_tracing_disabled

set_tracing_disabled(True)          # or export to your own collector; decide deliberately

@input_guardrail
async def topical(ctx, agent, user_input) -> GuardrailFunctionOutput:
    verdict = await cheap_classifier(user_input)      # small model, runs first
    return GuardrailFunctionOutput(
        output_info=verdict,
        tripwire_triggered=verdict.off_topic or verdict.jailbreak)

billing = Agent(name="Billing", instructions="Handle invoices only.", tools=[lookup])
triage = Agent(name="Triage", instructions="Route the customer.",
               handoffs=[billing],                    # transfers control
               input_guardrails=[topical])

try:
    result = await Runner.run(triage, user_text, max_turns=8)
except InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered:
    return "I can only help with account and billing questions."   # no expensive call made
followups: When do you use a handoff rather than calling an agent as a tool?
What happens when max_turns is reached, and what should the user see?
Where do sessions live once you run more than one instance?
What is the cost argument for guardrails, separate from the safety argument?
redflags: Leaves default tracing on with customer data
Guardrails implemented as instructions in the prompt
Assumes local session storage will scale
memory: Guardrails trip before you pay, handoffs move control, and default tracing and sessions both need a deliberate decision.

title: AutoGen, Semantic Kernel and Conversation-Driven Agents
question: A .NET-heavy enterprise wants agents, and someone suggests AutoGen because the multi-agent conversation demos look impressive. What do you warn them about?
technical: Conversation-driven multi-agent is the most expensive way to be non-deterministic. Agents that chat until they agree have no natural stopping point, so explicit termination conditions, a maximum message count and a cost ceiling are mandatory rather than tuning knobs.

The two Microsoft lineages solve different problems: AutoGen came from research into multi-agent conversation and is excellent for exploration, while Semantic Kernel came from enterprise application development with plugins, filters and first-class .NET and Java support. Microsoft has been converging them into a single agent framework, so a new build should target the converged path rather than the older ones.

For an enterprise the deciding factors are usually not agent cleverness: language support across .NET and Python, identity integration, network and data-residency constraints, OpenTelemetry that lands in the APM they already run, and a support relationship. Those matter more than which library has the nicer demo.

Whatever the framework, the production shape is the same: bound the loop, make tool calls idempotent, checkpoint long workflows so a crash resumes, and keep human approval in front of anything irreversible.

Watch out for demos that dissolve on contact with real data. Agents debating in a transcript looks like reasoning, but if the same result comes from one model call with two good tools, the multi-agent version is just a slower, costlier way to get there.
layman: A committee that keeps talking until everyone agrees will get there eventually, but nobody scheduled the end of the meeting and the room is charged by the hour.
code:
Interview focus:
- Conversation-based multi-agent needs explicit termination, message caps and a budget.
- AutoGen came from research on agent conversation; Semantic Kernel from enterprise
  application development with plugins and filters; Microsoft has been converging
  them into one agent framework, which is what a new build should target.
- The enterprise decision is usually language support, identity, data residency,
  OpenTelemetry into the existing APM, and support - not agent cleverness.
- Same production rules regardless of framework: bound the loop, idempotent tools,
  checkpoint long runs, human approval before anything irreversible.
followups: How does a group of chatting agents decide it is finished?
What would make you choose this stack over LangGraph or ADK?
How do you get these traces into the APM the company already pays for?
How would you prove the multi-agent version beats one agent with good tools?
redflags: No termination condition on a group chat
Chooses on demo quality rather than platform fit
No plan for tracing into existing monitoring

title: Choosing an Agent Framework You Will Not Regret
question: LangGraph, CrewAI, ADK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, or no framework at all. How do you actually make this decision, and how much does it cost you if you get it wrong?
technical: Start with the shape of the problem, not the library. A fixed process with a couple of judgement calls wants explicit orchestration; an open-ended task with tools wants a bounded agent loop; a single prompt with structured output wants no framework at all. Most production systems are the first or third, and are built as the second by mistake.

Then let the non-negotiables eliminate options: language, cloud and data residency, whether you need durable multi-day runs, human-in-the-loop, streaming, per-tenant isolation, and where traces are allowed to go. That list usually leaves two candidates, at which point ergonomics can decide.

Know what is actually portable. Prompts, tool implementations, evaluation datasets and business logic move between frameworks with modest effort. The orchestration graph, the state model and the runtime do not. So keep tools as plain functions with the framework wrapper on the outside, and the migration cost stays bounded.

Weigh the ecosystem honestly: tracing, evaluation, deployment targets, security review of transitive dependencies, and how quickly the API is still changing. A framework that moves fast is a running upgrade cost that someone has to own.

Judge with a spike, not a demo. Build the same nasty case in two candidates, including a tool failure, a human approval and a resume after a crash, and measure tokens, latency and how long debugging took. The framework that makes the ugly path clear is the right one.
layman: Choosing a delivery van by watching an advert on a smooth road tells you nothing. Load it up, drive it uphill in the rain, and see which one you can still service yourself.
usecases: Replacing a prototype that reached production
Justifying the choice to an architecture board
code:
Interview focus:
- Match the shape first: fixed process + judgement -> explicit orchestration;
  open-ended with tools -> bounded agent loop; one prompt -> no framework.
- Eliminate on non-negotiables: language, cloud, residency, durability,
  human-in-the-loop, streaming, tenant isolation, where traces may go.
- Portable: prompts, tools, eval datasets, business logic.
  Not portable: orchestration graph, state model, runtime.
  So write tools as plain functions and wrap them at the edge.
- Decide with a spike on the ugly path: tool failure, approval, crash + resume.
  Measure tokens, latency and debugging time - not demo quality.
followups: What would make you use no framework at all?
Which parts of your system would survive a framework migration untouched?
How do you stop three teams picking three different frameworks?
Your framework releases a breaking major version. What is the plan?
redflags: Picks on popularity or demo quality
No spike, only a proof of concept on the happy path
Framework calls spread through business logic
memory: Match the problem shape, eliminate on non-negotiables, keep tools plain, and decide with a spike on the ugly path.

title: When Framework Checkpointing Is Not Enough
question: Your agent workflow spans three days, calls four external systems and must survive deploys. Framework checkpointing is not covering it. What do you reach for?
technical: Framework checkpointers are built for a run: they persist graph state so a process can resume. A durable execution engine such as Temporal, Restate, Step Functions or Durable Functions is built for a business process: retries with backoff per activity, timers measured in days, signals from outside, versioning of running workflows and visibility into every one in flight.

The split that works is orchestration outside, intelligence inside. Workflow code stays deterministic and does no model calls; every model call, tool call and database write is an activity with its own timeout and retry policy. The agent loop becomes an activity, or a child workflow when it needs its own steps.

That determinism rule is the part teams get wrong. Random values, timestamps and non-deterministic library calls in workflow code break replay, and an LLM is the least deterministic thing there is, which is exactly why it belongs behind an activity boundary.

Long processes need compensation, not just retries. Three days in, step four fails and step two already sent money, so you need a saga that reverses or escalates, plus idempotency keys everywhere, because at-least-once delivery means activities re-run.

Human steps become first-class: a signal or an update wakes the workflow when an approval arrives, with a durable timer that escalates if nobody responds. That is far more robust than a row in a table and a cron job, and it is visible in one place when someone asks where a case is stuck.
layman: A recipe card helps you resume cooking after a phone call. Running a restaurant for three days needs a rota, a booking system and someone who notices an order never came back from the kitchen.
usecases: Agents that wait days for a human or an external system
Anything an auditor will ask to trace end to end
followups: Why can the model call not live in workflow code?
Step four fails after step two moved money. What happens?
How do you deploy a change while thousands of workflows are mid-flight?
When is framework checkpointing genuinely sufficient?
redflags: Model calls inside deterministic workflow code
Multi-day waits implemented with sleeps or cron
No way to list workflows currently stuck
memory: Durable engine outside for retries, timers, signals and versioning; the agent inside an activity, with sagas for what cannot be retried.

title: Running Guardrails Without Wrecking Latency
question: You add moderation, jailbreak detection and PII checks around your agent, and now every answer takes two seconds longer and support is complaining about false blocks. How do you build this properly?
technical: Layer by cost and place each check where it pays. Cheap deterministic checks first, regex and allow-lists and length limits; then a small classifier for jailbreak and topicality on the input; then policy at the tool boundary; then an output check for leakage. A large model as a judge on every request is the expensive last resort, not the first line.

Spend latency in parallel, not in series. Input checks run alongside the first model call and cancel it on a trip; output checks on a streamed response run per chunk with a small buffer so nothing reaches the screen unchecked, rather than holding the whole answer back.

False positives are a product decision with a cost. Measure the block rate against sampled human labels, tune per surface rather than globally, and prefer a clarifying reply over a hard refusal when confidence is middling. A guardrail nobody trusts gets switched off, which is worse than a slightly leaky one.

The real enforcement point is the tool, not the text. Instructions in a prompt are advisory; permission checks, argument validation and spend limits inside the tool are what actually stop an injected instruction from doing damage, which matters more as tool results feed back into context.

Treat it as a living control: log every trip with enough context to review, keep a red-team set that grows with each new bypass, re-run it on model and prompt changes, and be careful about where blocked content is stored, since that store now holds the worst inputs you have ever received.
layman: Airport security works because the quick checks come first and only a few bags get opened. Hand-searching every suitcase would be safer and nobody would ever catch a flight.
usecases: Agents with tools that can act
Defending against prompt injection through retrieved content
followups: Which check catches an injection that arrives inside a retrieved document?
How do you moderate a streamed answer without buffering all of it?
What is your false-positive rate, and how do you know?
Where do you store blocked content, and for how long?
redflags: A large judge model on every request
Guardrails only in the system prompt
Blocked content logged with no retention thought
memory: Cheap checks first and in parallel, enforcement at the tool boundary, and measure false positives or it gets turned off.

title: Managed Agent Runtimes and What They Cost You
question: Vertex AI Agent Engine, Bedrock AgentCore, LangGraph Platform, Azure AI Foundry. When is a managed agent runtime worth it, and what are you giving up?
technical: What you are buying is the boring infrastructure: session and thread persistence, long-running executions that outlive an HTTP request, per-session isolation, scaling to zero, background runs and schedules, identity plumbing and tracing already wired in. Building that yourself is several months of platform work that has nothing to do with your product.

What you give up is portability and visibility. The runtime holds your session model and its scaling behaviour, debugging happens through their console, quotas and regional availability become your constraints, and the exit cost lands squarely on the orchestration layer, which is the least portable part of the system.

The economics turn on shape of load. Spiky, session-heavy, long-running workloads suit a managed runtime; steady high-throughput traffic on infrastructure you already run often does not, and per-session pricing can quietly exceed a small always-on service.

Compliance decides more of this than architecture does. Where sessions and memory are stored, which regions exist, what the retention and deletion story is, and whether prompts crossing into a managed service is acceptable at all: settle those before evaluating features.

The hedge is the same in every case: keep tools, prompts and evaluation datasets outside the runtime as ordinary code and data, and treat the runtime as deployment target rather than the home of your business logic. Then a move is a redeploy, not a rewrite.
layman: Renting a fully serviced office gets you working on Monday. It is a genuinely good deal until you need to knock a wall through, and moving out means packing everything you put in the fitted cupboards.
usecases: Getting a pilot in front of users quickly
code:
Interview focus:
- Buying: session/thread persistence, long runs past request timeouts, session
  isolation, scale to zero, background runs and schedules, identity, tracing.
- Giving up: portability of the orchestration layer, debugging outside your
  own tooling, quotas and regional limits, per-session cost at scale.
- Economics: spiky and session-heavy suits managed; steady high throughput on
  infrastructure you already run usually does not.
- Compliance first: where sessions and memory live, regions, retention, deletion.
- Hedge: tools, prompts and eval datasets stay outside as ordinary code and data;
  the runtime is a deployment target, not where business logic lives.
followups: What exactly would you have to rewrite to move off it?
How do you debug a failing run when the runtime is not yours?
At what traffic level does self-hosting become cheaper?
What does the runtime store, and can you delete one user's data from it?
redflags: Adopts on convenience with no exit analysis
Business logic written inside the runtime's abstractions
No check on region availability or quotas
Cannot answer where session data is stored
memory: Managed runtimes sell you the boring infrastructure and charge you in portability: keep tools, prompts and evals outside.

title: What Credentials Should an Agent Actually Hold?
question: Your agent needs to read orders, issue refunds and email customers. Someone gives it a service account with all three permissions permanently. What is wrong with that, and what does good look like?
technical: A standing account with the union of every permission is the worst case: one successful prompt injection now has all of it, and the audit log shows the service account rather than the person, so you cannot answer who authorised a refund.

Act on behalf of the user, not instead of them. Exchange the user's session for a short-lived, scoped token per action, so the agent can never do something the user could not do themselves, and the trail carries the real identity through to the downstream system.

Scope credentials per tool, per tenant and per run. Read tools get read tokens, the refund tool gets a token minted only after approval and only for that order, and tokens expire in minutes rather than living in the environment for the lifetime of the pod.

The classic failure is the confused deputy: content the agent reads instructs it to use its own privileges for something the user never asked for. Nothing in the prompt layer prevents that, so the tool itself must re-check who the actor is and what policy allows, on every call.

Log the authorisation decision, not only the action: which identity, which scope, which policy allowed it, which approval covered it. That is what makes an incident reviewable and what an auditor will ask for the moment an agent touches money.
layman: You would not give a new contractor a master key to the building because they occasionally need the stockroom. They get a badge that opens that door, during their shift, with their name on the log.
usecases: Agents calling internal APIs and MCP servers
Anything touching money, PII or production data
code:
# BAD: standing credentials with the union of every permission
agent = Agent(tools=[orders, refunds, email], creds=SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ALL)

# BETTER: short-lived, scoped, on behalf of the actual user
def refund_tool(order_id: str, amount: int, *, ctx: ToolContext):
    actor = ctx.user                                  # the human, not the agent
    if not policy.allows(actor, "refunds:write", order_id):
        return "Not permitted for this user."         # re-checked at the tool
    if amount > POLICY_LIMIT and not ctx.approval_id:
        return "Needs supervisor approval."

    token = sts.exchange(subject_token=ctx.user_token,   # on-behalf-of
                         scope="refunds:write",
                         resource=f"order/{order_id}",
                         ttl_seconds=120)                # minutes, not months
    resp = payments.refund(order_id, amount, token=token,
                           idempotency_key=f"{ctx.run_id}:{order_id}")
    audit.write(actor=actor, action="refund", order=order_id,
                amount=amount, policy="refunds:write",
                approval=ctx.approval_id, run=ctx.run_id)
    return resp
