Who appears in the audit log when the agent acts, and is that enough?
How do you scope credentials in a multi-tenant deployment?
Which actions require approval, and who decides that list?
redflags: One service account holding every permission
Permission checks only in the prompt
Audit log shows the agent rather than the user
No approval step for irreversible actions
memory: Short-lived scoped tokens on behalf of the user, re-checked inside the tool, with the human identity in the audit trail.

title: Agent Observability Without Vendor Lock-In
question: Your agent traces live in one AI tool, your application traces in the company APM, and during an incident nobody can tell which is which. How do you fix that?
technical: One request should be one trace. Agent spans belong under the same trace as the HTTP request, the database calls and the downstream services, which means propagating the trace context into the agent rather than starting a separate trace in a separate tool.

Use the OpenTelemetry generative-AI conventions as the common vocabulary: model, provider, token counts, tool name, run id. Once the spans carry standard attributes, they can be exported to more than one backend and can be queried alongside everything else you already monitor.

Most agent tracing tools are OpenTelemetry-compatible in one direction or another, so instrument once and export where it is useful: the AI-specific tool for prompt-level debugging and evaluation, the existing APM for latency, errors and correlation with the rest of the system.

Design the attributes you will need before the incident: tenant, user, request id, prompt version, model version, agent name, step index, tokens and cost per span. Those are what turn a trace from a story into a query you can aggregate over.

Mind what you put in span attributes. Full prompts and tool payloads mean your APM now stores customer data under a different retention policy, so redact at the exporter and decide deliberately what is captured at each level.
layman: Two sets of CCTV with different clocks and no shared labels. Neither is wrong, and together they still cannot tell you what happened.
usecases: Incidents spanning app and model calls
Cost attribution per tenant or feature
Comparing model or prompt versions in production
Companies with an existing APM investment
code:
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("agent")

def handle(request):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("http.request") as span:      # one trace
        span.set_attribute("tenant.id", request.tenant)
        return run_agent(request, ctx=trace.get_current_span())      # context flows in

def call_model(messages, ctx):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat", context=ctx) as span:
        span.set_attributes({
            "gen_ai.system": "anthropic",
            "gen_ai.request.model": MODEL,
            "gen_ai.usage.input_tokens": usage.input,
            "gen_ai.usage.output_tokens": usage.output,
            "app.prompt_version": PROMPT_V,
            "app.run_id": run_id,
        })
        # prompts are NOT attributes by default: redact or sample deliberately

# export once, fan out: AI tool for prompt debugging, APM for latency and errors
followups: How does a trace id get from the load balancer into an agent step?
Which attributes do you need to answer cost per tenant?
What do you deliberately not put in a span, and why?
How do you avoid instrumenting twice when you change agent tooling?
redflags: Separate traces for app and agent
Full prompts written into APM attributes
Instrumentation tied to one vendor's SDK
memory: One trace per request, standard generative-AI attributes, export to more than one backend, and redact before the span leaves.

title: OpenClaw and the Single-Operator Trust Boundary
question: Your team wants to run one OpenClaw instance for the whole department, wired into the shared Slack workspace. Why is that the wrong shape, and what is the right one?
technical: OpenClaw is designed around one trusted operator per gateway. It is a personal assistant model, not a multi-tenant security boundary, so anyone allowed to message a shared instance can trigger tools that run with that instance's privileges and credentials. Separate trust boundaries mean separate gateways, ideally separate hosts or OS users.

Order the controls: identity, then scope, then the model. Decide who may talk to it using pairing or an allowlist, then constrain where it can act with tool policies, group mention requirements and sandboxing, and only then think about how well the model resists manipulation. Reversing that order is how people end up relying on a system prompt for access control.

Session scoping is a real leak path. Without per-peer session scope, several people messaging the same assistant can share context, so one person's conversation becomes visible in another's. In a shared workspace that is a data incident with no exploit required.

The dangerous defaults are the convenient ones. Open DM policy, no mention requirement in groups, and high-blast-radius tools such as shell execution, browser control and web fetch left enabled together turn an ordinary message into arbitrary action on the host.

For a team use case the correct answer is usually a different product: a service-shaped agent with real authentication, per-user authorisation and an audit trail. A personal assistant scaled to a department is not an enterprise deployment, it is a shared root account with a chat interface.
layman: A house key you happily give to your own assistant is not something you photocopy for the whole floor. Everyone would be able to open your front door, and the log would just say the key was used.
usecases: Evaluating a personal agent for team use
Security review of a self-hosted assistant
Choosing between personal and service-shaped agents
Setting policy for autonomous assistants at work
followups: Two colleagues message the same assistant. What stops one seeing the other's context?
What is the difference between a pairing policy and an allowlist?
Which tools would you deny by default, and why those?
When is a personal agent simply the wrong tool for the job?
redflags: One shared instance for many users
Access control expressed in the system prompt
Open DM policy with execution tools enabled
Assumes a personal assistant is a multi-tenant platform
memory: One operator, one gateway: identity first, scope second, model last, and a shared instance is a shared privilege set.

title: Hardening a Self-Hosted Agent Gateway
question: Security researchers keep finding OpenClaw gateways exposed on the public internet, some over plain HTTP with no authentication. Walk me through hardening one properly.
technical: The exposure itself is the incident. A gateway bound to all interfaces without authentication is a remote shell with a chat interface attached, and over plain HTTP the traffic and any bearer token travel in the clear. Bind to loopback, reach it through a VPN or an identity-aware proxy, and require a token or proxy-provided identity.

State on disk is the second prize. Configuration, channel credentials, OAuth tokens and full session transcripts live in the agent's state directory, so directory and file permissions matter, and those transcripts should be treated as confidential customer data with a retention policy rather than as logs.

Sandboxing is opt-in, which produces a specific and common failure: a container backend configured while sandbox mode is still off, so tools run on the host anyway. Audit for that drift rather than trusting that configuring something meant enabling it.

Use the built-in security audit as a control, not a curiosity. Run it in the deployment pipeline, fail the deploy on critical findings, and re-run it after upgrades, because a fast-moving project changes defaults between releases.

Then assume compromise anyway: separate the browser profile from personal accounts, keep secrets out of the filesystem the agent can read, give it scoped tokens rather than your own long-lived credentials, and put egress controls in front of the host so exfiltration is not a single HTTP call away.
layman: Leaving the gateway open to the internet is not a weak lock on the front door. It is the front door removed, with a note explaining where the valuables are.
usecases: Deploying a self-hosted agent on a VPS
Security review before allowing an agent on the network
Incident response after an exposed instance
Writing a hardening standard for autonomous assistants
code:
# 1. never publicly bound; reach it over a private network
gateway.bind = loopback          # or a Tailscale-style identity-aware proxy
gateway.auth = token             # long random; rotate on staff change

# 2. lock down the state directory: config, channel creds, OAuth tokens, transcripts
chmod 700 ~/.openclaw
chmod 600 ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json
# ~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/sessions/*.jsonl  <- full transcripts: confidential + retention

# 3. catch policy drift: sandbox backend configured but mode still off
openclaw security audit          # config checks
openclaw security audit --deep   # live probe of the running gateway
#   run in CI, fail the deploy on critical findings, re-run after every upgrade

# 4. assume compromise: scoped tokens, separate browser profile, egress allowlist
followups: What is in the state directory, and which of it would hurt most if leaked?
How would you detect an exposed instance across the estate?
The sandbox is configured but disabled. How would you notice?
Which credentials should the agent never hold at all?
redflags: Plain HTTP with a bearer token
Uses the operator's personal long-lived credentials
memory: Loopback plus real authentication, locked-down state, sandbox actually enabled, audit in CI, and scoped credentials on the assumption of compromise.

title: Injection Through the Things an Agent Reads
question: An OpenClaw agent was told in a Discord message to repeat the last message from every channel, and it did, leaking private moderator conversations. Nobody had access to the host. How do you design so that this is survivable?
technical: There are two doors, and the second is the dangerous one. Direct injection arrives in a message someone sends the agent; indirect injection arrives inside content the agent reads on your behalf, and there are documented cases of instructions planted in public posts aimed at agents, including ones written to drain crypto wallets. Anything the agent ingests is untrusted input.

Model robustness helps but is the last line, not the plan. Vendor-run injection arenas put frontier models at roughly one percent success across hundreds of thousands of attempts, which is low and is not zero at the volume of messages a live agent reads, and older or smaller models are markedly easier to steer.

Design for blast radius instead. Deny high-risk tools by default, especially shell execution, browser control and arbitrary web fetch in the same profile that reads untrusted content, and require an explicit mention before the agent acts on anything in a group.

Split the agent by trust level. A read-only profile with a restricted tool policy handles untrusted content and returns a summary; the acting agent, which holds credentials, never reads raw external text. That separation is what stops a sentence in a forum post from becoming a tool call.

Then instrument the boundary: log every tool call with the content that triggered it, alert on unusual sequences such as a read followed by a bulk send, and keep an approval step in front of anything irreversible or anything that leaves the organisation.
layman: A shop assistant who follows any instruction shouted from the street. You do not fix that by hiring someone more sceptical; you make sure the till and the safe are not reachable from the pavement.
usecases: Agents that browse or read email
code:
# two profiles, two trust levels

reader:                       # touches untrusted content, holds nothing
  tools: [web_fetch, read_channel]
  deny:  [exec, browser, send_message, group:automation]
  credentials: none
  output: summary_only        # returns text, never a tool request

actor:                        # holds credentials, never reads raw external text
  tools: [send_message, calendar_write]
  input: reader.summary_only  # structured, length-capped, no raw markup
  approval_required: [payments, mass_send, external_email]

# detection: the shape of an exfiltration is a read fan-in then a send fan-out
alert when tool_calls matches: read_* {3,} -> send_* within 60s
followups: Which is more dangerous, a message sent to the agent or a document it reads? Why?
Where exactly does the untrusted text stop in your design?
How would you catch this in the logs after the fact?
The model resists injection ninety-nine percent of the time. Is that good enough here?
redflags: One profile that both reads untrusted content and holds credentials
Execution and browser tools enabled alongside reading
Treats prompt injection as a model problem rather than a design one
memory: Untrusted input reaches an agent through everything it reads: split reading from acting, deny the dangerous tools, and design the blast radius.

title: Agent Skills Are a Supply Chain
question: Your agent platform lets anyone install community skills, and one published scan found roughly a quarter of thirty thousand skills carried at least one vulnerability. How do you allow skills without importing that risk?
technical: A skill is executable code plus instructions that run with the agent's privileges, which makes it a dependency in the strictest sense. It deserves the same treatment as a library: a known source, a pinned version, a review, and an owner who notices when it changes.

Portability standards make skills shareable between agents, which is genuinely useful and also means a bad skill travels. Curate an internal allowlist rather than enabling a public catalogue wholesale, and mirror what you approve so upstream cannot mutate under you.

The instruction half is as dangerous as the code half. A skill's prose runs inside the model's context, so it can quietly redirect behaviour without a single suspicious line of code, and a review that only reads the Python misses it entirely.

Scan and re-scan: static checks for network and filesystem calls, secret access and shell invocation, plus a diff review on every version bump. Automated skill scanners exist and do find real issues, but they are a filter rather than a substitute for an owner.

Contain what you cannot fully vet. Run skills in the sandbox rather than on the host, give each one only the tools and credentials it needs, and log skill invocations separately so an incident can be traced to the exact skill and version.
layman: Installing a community skill is closer to hiring a contractor with keys than to downloading a wallpaper. You would at least ask who they are and what they intend to touch.
usecases: Platforms with plugin or skill ecosystems
Responding to a compromised upstream skill
code:
Interview focus:
- A skill is code plus prompt text running with the agent's privileges: treat it as
  a dependency, with a source, pinned version, review and an owner.
- Review both halves. The instruction text runs in the model's context and can
  redirect behaviour with no suspicious code at all.
- Curate an internal allowlist and mirror approved versions rather than enabling
  a public catalogue; portability means a bad skill travels well.
- Scan for network, filesystem, secret and shell access; diff every version bump.
  Scanners are a filter, not an owner.
- Contain the rest: run skills sandboxed, scope credentials per skill, and log
  invocations with skill name and version so incidents are traceable.
followups: What do you look for when reviewing a skill, beyond the code?
An approved skill publishes a new version overnight. What happens?
How do you scope credentials per skill rather than per agent?
How would you trace an incident back to a specific skill and version?
redflags: Reviews only the code and not the instructions
Skills run on the host with the agent's full credentials
memory: Skills are dependencies that run with your privileges: allowlist, pin, review both code and prose, sandbox, and log by version.

title: Hermes Agent: Operating Something That Rewrites Itself
question: Hermes Agent curates its own memory and writes its own reusable skills, improving them as it goes. What does that closed loop break in your normal production practices?
technical: Your deployed artefact is no longer the thing you reviewed. An agent that writes and refines its own skills is generating code that will run later with real privileges, so skill creation needs the same gate as any other code path reaching production: a diff, a reviewer, a version, and the ability to roll back to yesterday's behaviour.

Memory becomes persistent state that shapes every future run, which makes memory poisoning a durable attack rather than a single bad answer. Something false written into memory today is retrieved and acted on for weeks, so memory needs provenance, review of what gets promoted to long-term, and a way to expire or excise an entry.

Evaluation has to be continuous because the system changes without a deploy. Pin a golden dataset and re-run it on a schedule rather than only on release, because the thing that regressed may be a skill the agent wrote at 3am rather than a commit anyone made.

Debugging shifts from reading code to reading history. When behaviour changes you need to know which memory entries and which skill versions were in play for that run, which means capturing them per run rather than reconstructing later from a mutable store.

Decide deliberately how much autonomy the loop gets. Self-improvement is genuinely valuable for a single user's personal workflows and much harder to justify where the output touches customers or money, so the safe pattern is autonomous drafting with human promotion, not autonomous deployment.
layman: An assistant who rewrites their own job description every night is wonderful until something goes wrong, because the job description you approved is not the one they are working to.
usecases: Personal productivity agents that persist across sessions
Assessing autonomy levels for a business process
Debugging behaviour that changed with no code change
code:
Interview focus:
- Self-written skills are code reaching production: require review, versioning
  and rollback before a generated skill is allowed to run with real privileges.
- Memory is durable state, so poisoning persists. Track provenance, gate what is
  promoted to long-term, and support expiry and excision of entries.
- Evaluate continuously, not per release: the regression may be a skill the agent
  wrote overnight rather than a commit.
- Capture memory entries and skill versions per run, or you cannot explain why
  today's behaviour differs from yesterday's.
- Prefer autonomous drafting with human promotion wherever output touches
  customers or money; full self-deployment is a personal-use pattern.
followups: A skill the agent wrote last week starts failing. How do you find and fix it?
How does false information get into memory, and how does it get out?
What would you refuse to let the agent self-improve?
How do you evaluate a system whose behaviour changes without a deploy?
redflags: No provenance or expiry on memory
Cannot say which skill version produced a given run
memory: If it writes its own skills and memory, then review, version and expiry apply to those too: draft autonomously, promote deliberately.

title: Unattended Agent Runs and Scheduled Jobs
question: Your agent has a built-in scheduler and now runs jobs at three in the morning with nobody watching. What has to be true before you turn that on?
technical: Unattended means the human control you were relying on is gone. Any step that would have paused for approval now either blocks forever or proceeds without one, so decide per action which it is, and make the blocked case visible in the morning rather than silently stuck.

Scheduled runs need the same discipline as any batch job: idempotency so a retry does not duplicate work, a lock so an overrun does not overlap the next run, a timeout, a bounded retry policy, and an alert when a run fails or produces nothing.

Cost has no natural ceiling overnight. A loop that would have annoyed a watching user simply bills until morning, so a per-run token and wall-clock budget with a hard stop is mandatory, along with a daily cap across all scheduled work.

Credentials are exposed for longer and used without a human present, which makes short-lived scoped tokens and a narrow tool profile more important, not less. Do not let the overnight job hold more permission than the interactive one.

Choose the isolation backend for the job rather than for convenience. Local execution is the fastest way to have an unattended agent modify the host it runs on; containerised or remote sandbox backends give a clean environment per run and make blast radius a configuration choice.
layman: Giving someone a key to work overnight is fine. Giving them the key, the company card and no way to reach you when something looks odd is a different decision.
usecases: Scheduled research, reporting or monitoring agents
Any agent with a cron feature enabled
code:
Interview focus:
- Unattended removes the human in the loop: decide per action whether it blocks
  and surfaces in the morning, or proceeds without approval. Never silent-stuck.
- Batch discipline: idempotency key per run, a lock against overlap, a timeout,
  bounded retries, and an alert on failure or empty output.
- Budgets are mandatory overnight: per-run token and wall-clock ceiling plus a
  daily cap across all scheduled work.
- Credentials: short-lived and scoped; the overnight job gets no more permission
  than the interactive one, and ideally less.
- Isolation: pick a container or remote sandbox backend per run rather than local
  execution on the host the agent can modify.
followups: A scheduled run needs approval at 3am. What happens?
The job runs long and the next one starts. What did you put in place?
How do you cap spend across every scheduled agent?
Which backend would you run it on, and why?
redflags: Overnight jobs holding broader credentials than interactive use
Local execution on the host for unattended work
memory: Unattended removes the human safeguard: budgets, locks, idempotency, scoped credentials and a clean sandbox per run replace it.

title: Employees Running Personal Agents on Work Data
question: An open-source personal agent goes viral, reaching a quarter of a million GitHub stars in two months, and your engineers are running it on work laptops connected to their own messaging accounts. What do you do on Monday?
technical: Understand the actual exposure before writing policy. This is software on a managed device holding channel credentials and reading corporate content, then routing it through an operator-controlled host and a personal messaging account, which is a data egress path that no existing control was designed to see.

Inventory first: detect installations and running gateways across the fleet, and look outward too, since exposed instances are discoverable from the internet and yours may already be indexed. You cannot govern what you have not found.

Then decide policy on the basis of risk rather than novelty. A blanket ban drives it underground on personal machines where you have no visibility at all, so the workable answer is usually a sanctioned path: approved deployment pattern, hardened configuration, no corporate credentials, no customer data, and clear red lines about what an agent may never touch.

Add runtime controls where they fit your estate: egress restrictions from developer machines, alerting on agent-shaped traffic, credential hygiene so no personal tool holds a long-lived corporate token, and behavioural monitoring for anomalous tool use rather than trusting the tool to police itself.

Treat it as a governance question with an owner and a review date, because this class of tool moves fast enough that a decision made this quarter will be out of date next quarter. Naming what is allowed and giving people a supported alternative beats a memo nobody can comply with.
layman: Staff have started bringing in a very capable new intern from home who reads their work mail and does favours. Banning them outright just moves the arrangement off-site; the answer is to define what the intern may see and where they may sit.
usecases: Enabling AI productivity without uncontrolled egress
code:
Interview focus:
- Exposure: agent software on managed devices, holding channel credentials, reading
  corporate content, routed through a personal account. A new egress path nothing
  was designed to observe.
- Inventory first, inside and out: fleet detection of installs and running gateways,
  plus external scanning, because exposed instances are discoverable.
- Policy on risk, not novelty. A blanket ban moves it to unmanaged machines; offer a
  sanctioned pattern: hardened config, no corporate credentials, no customer data,
  explicit red lines.
- Runtime controls: egress restrictions, alerting on agent-shaped traffic, credential
  hygiene, behavioural monitoring of tool use.
- Governance with an owner and a review date; this class of tool changes quarterly.
followups: How would you find every instance running in the company?
Would you ban it? Argue the case either way.
What is the sanctioned alternative you offer instead?
Which single control reduces the most risk here?
redflags: Bans it with no alternative and assumes compliance
Treats it as an IT annoyance rather than a data egress path
No red lines about credentials or customer data
Policy with no owner or review date
memory: Find it, then offer a hardened sanctioned path with hard red lines: a ban without an alternative just removes your visibility.

title: Operating a Fast-Moving Open-Source Agent
question: The agent project you have deployed ships breaking changes weekly and grew faster than any project in open-source history. How do you run it without either freezing on an old version or chasing every release?
technical: Pin a version and upgrade on a cadence you choose. Track releases for security fixes specifically, and separate those from feature releases so an urgent patch is not entangled with a configuration overhaul you have not reviewed.

Re-run the security audit and your own configuration checks after every upgrade, because on a project moving this fast the defaults themselves change, and a setting you deliberately hardened can be replaced or renamed underneath you.

Back up the state that matters and know what restore looks like: configuration, channel pairings and credentials, memory or skill stores, and scheduled jobs. Losing the state directory usually means re-pairing every channel by hand, which is an outage nobody planned for.

Keep an exit and a rollback. Configuration and skills in version control, state backed up before every upgrade, and a tested downgrade path, since a fast-moving project will eventually ship a release that does not work for your setup.

Watch it like a service rather than a gadget: health of the gateway, failed and overdue scheduled runs, token spend per day, tool-call volume and error rates. Most incidents with these tools are noticed by someone's surprise rather than by monitoring, which is the real gap.
layman: Living on the newest version of everything is exhausting, and never updating is how you end up with a system nobody can patch. You pick an upgrade day and you keep a way back.
usecases: Setting an upgrade policy for AI tooling
Monitoring an agent as a production service
code:
Interview focus:
- Pin the version; upgrade on your own cadence. Track security releases separately
  from feature releases so an urgent fix is not bundled with a config overhaul.
- Re-run the security audit after every upgrade: on fast projects the defaults move,
  and hardened settings get renamed or replaced.
- Back up what cannot be rebuilt: config, channel pairings and credentials, memory
  and skill stores, scheduled jobs. Losing state means re-pairing every channel.
- Keep config and skills in version control, snapshot state before upgrading, and
  test the downgrade path before you need it.
- Monitor as a service: gateway health, failed or overdue scheduled runs, daily token
  spend, tool-call volume and error rate.
followups: How do you tell a security release from a feature release quickly?
The state directory is lost. What is the recovery?
An upgrade breaks your configuration. What is the rollback?
What do you alert on for an agent like this?
redflags: No backup of the state directory
No monitoring of scheduled runs or spend
memory: Pin, upgrade on a cadence, re-audit after every upgrade, back up the state that cannot be rebuilt, and monitor it like a service.

title: LLMOps: Shipping and Operating LLM Systems
question: What does LLMOps have to deal with that DevOps and MLOps do not? And how do you get a prompt or model change into production safely?
technical: The deployable unit is a bundle: model version + prompt version + tool definitions + retrieval index version + parameters — any one changing changes behaviour, so version and release them together.
Prompts are code: reviewed, versioned, tested in CI against an eval suite with gates (task quality, safety, cost, latency) before any deploy — never edited live in a dashboard.

Release like any risky change: offline evals, then shadow or canary traffic scored against the incumbent, then progressive rollout with automatic rollback triggers on quality, refusal-rate or cost regressions.
Providers are dependencies you don't control: pin model versions, test provider updates like upgrades, and keep a tested fallback (secondary provider or self-hosted) with capacity and quota alarms.

Close the loop: production traces feed the eval set (hard cases become regression tests), incidents get playbooks (quality regression is an incident class, not a vibe), and cost budgets are enforced per feature.
layman: A restaurant chain changing a recipe: the new sauce is written down and versioned, taste-tested against the old one, tried in three restaurants first, and rolled back by the book if complaints rise — nobody re-seasons the pot live in one kitchen.
code:
release_bundle:
  model: gemini-2.5-pro @ pinned
  prompt: support-agent v41
  tools: v12         # schemas versioned with prompt
  index: v7
pipeline: evals(gate) -> shadow(24h) -> canary(5%) -> rollout(25/50/100)
rollback_on: [quality < baseline-2%, refusals > 2x, cost > 1.3x]
followups: What exactly is in your deployable unit?
How do you catch a silent provider model update?
What triggers automatic rollback?
How do production failures become regression tests?
redflags: No canary or rollback for prompt changes
memory: Version the bundle — model, prompt, tools, index — gate with evals, roll out progressively, and feed failures back into the eval set.

title: LLM Observability: Tracing, Drift and Quality Monitoring
question: Your monitoring says the request was fast and returned a 200, and the answer was still wrong. What does observability look like for an LLM system in production?
technical: Trace the full generation path per request: prompt version, model, parameters, token counts, latency split (TTFT/decode), tool calls with inputs and outputs, retrieval chunks used, and final response — a bad answer must be reconstructable.

Quality is a sampled, scored signal: run LLM-judge scoring on a sample of live traffic against rubrics (groundedness, task success, tone), calibrated periodically with human labels — 200 OK says nothing about correctness.

Watch drift on both sides: input drift (topic mix, language, prompt-injection attempts) and output drift (length, refusal rate, format breakage, citation rate) — provider-side model updates often show up here first.
Wire user signals into the timeline: thumbs, edits, retries, abandonment and escalation-to-human are the cheapest ground truth you have; segment all metrics by feature, tenant and model version.
Logs contain user content: apply PII redaction, retention limits and access control to traces — observability must not become the leak.
layman: A call centre where every call connects fine: dashboards show connection time, but you still need supervisors listening to a sample of calls, complaint rates per team, and recordings handled under strict privacy rules — connected is not the same as helped.
followups: How would you debug one wrong answer from last Tuesday?
How is the LLM judge itself kept honest?
Which metric catches a silent provider model change first?
Who can read traces, and what was redacted?
redflags: Only infrastructure metrics, no quality signal
No trace linking answer to prompt/model/chunks
Raw user content in logs forever
Judge scores never calibrated with humans
memory: Trace every generation end-to-end, score sampled quality, watch input and output drift, and treat traces as sensitive data.

title: Business Requirements vs Technical Implementation Details
question: When planning a generative AI solution, which factors belong in the business case as core requirements, and which are technical implementation details? Classify these: a CSAT target, model choice, ticket deflection rate, context window size, cost per resolved conversation, RAG vs fine-tuning.
technical: Core business requirements state the outcome without naming any technology: a target CSAT or NPS movement, ticket deflection or containment rate, average handle time, first-contact resolution, cost per resolved conversation, revenue or conversion impact, plus hard constraints such as regulatory compliance, data residency, brand voice and supported languages.

Technical implementation details are the choices engineering makes to hit those numbers, and they can change without re-opening the business case: model family and size, RAG vs fine-tuning, embedding model, chunking strategy, vector store, prompt design, token budgets, serving hardware.

The classification test: if changing it forces the sponsor to re-approve the business case, it is a requirement; if the team can swap it mid-sprint while the metrics hold, it is an implementation detail.
Requirements must be measurable and baselined before anything is built: today's CSAT, today's cost per ticket, today's handle time. A project without a baseline cannot prove it worked.

Exam framing: among options like 'which model to use', 'embedding dimensionality', 'vector database choice' and 'target customer satisfaction score', the core business requirement is the CSAT target; everything else is implementation.
layman: A restaurant owner specifies 'diners rate us 4.5 stars and a meal costs under 8 pounds to make'. Which oven the chef buys is the chef's call, and swapping ovens never needs the owner's signature.
usecases: Writing the business case for a gen AI assistant
Scoping a support-bot pilot with a sponsor
Certification and interview questions on solution planning
Steering-committee updates that survive a model swap
code:
Requirement sheet, two columns:

Business requirement (sponsor signs)   Technical detail (team decides)
CSAT +0.3 on assisted chats            model family and size
30% tier-1 ticket deflection           RAG vs fine-tuning
cost per resolved chat under $0.40     embedding model, chunk size
answers only from the approved KB      vector store, reranker
PII never leaves the region            prompt template, token budget
followups: Which of your requirements is a constraint rather than a target, and what happens when a target and a constraint conflict?
How would you baseline CSAT before launch?
Who owns a requirement after launch: product or platform?
redflags: The business case names a model or a vector database
Success defined as 'launch the chatbot' with no measurable target
No baseline measured before the pilot starts
memory: The sponsor buys outcomes (CSAT, deflection, cost); engineering picks the machinery.

title: Business KPIs for Generative AI: CSAT, Deflection, Cost per Resolution
question: Name the business KPIs a generative AI assistant is typically judged on, and explain which are leading and which are lagging.
technical: Customer satisfaction: CSAT (post-interaction survey, share satisfied) and NPS (would you recommend, scored -100 to +100). Both are lagging: they move weeks after quality changes and are diluted by everything else the company does.

Workload KPIs: deflection or containment rate (share of contacts resolved with no human), first-contact resolution, average handle time, escalation rate. These lead CSAT and are measurable per conversation, per week.

Economics: cost per resolved conversation, all-in (tokens, infrastructure, and the human escalations it still causes) against the human-only baseline. Margin per interaction is the number finance signs.
Adoption and trust: weekly active users, retry and abandonment rates, thumbs-down rate, and for agent-assist tools the acceptance rate (how often the human keeps the drafted answer).
Every KPI needs a baseline and a counterfactual (an A/B or a holdout group), or the improvement will be claimed by whoever shipped anything that quarter.
layman: A clinic judges a new triage nurse two ways: patient satisfaction surveys, which arrive months later, and how many patients were sorted correctly today. You steer with today's numbers and prove value with the survey.
usecases: Quarterly business review for an AI assistant
Choosing what the executive dashboard shows
code:
KPI sheet with baselines:

KPI                        baseline   target    cadence   type
CSAT (assisted chats)      3.9 / 5    4.2 / 5   monthly   lagging
deflection rate            0%         30%       weekly    leading
first-contact resolution   62%        70%       weekly    leading
cost per resolved chat     $4.10      $0.40     weekly    leading
escalation complaints      n/a        under 2%  weekly    guardrail
followups: Why can deflection rise while CSAT falls, and which guardrail catches it?
What is a containment rate worth if the contained users simply gave up?
What survey response rate makes a CSAT movement believable?
redflags: Deflection celebrated without a 'was it actually resolved' check
CSAT quoted from a 3% survey response rate with no honesty band
Only token spend reported, never cost per resolution
memory: Steer weekly with deflection, resolution and cost; prove quarterly with CSAT.

title: The Metric Chain: Business KPI to Online Proxy to Offline Eval
question: Your sponsor cares about CSAT. Your CI pipeline scores groundedness. Connect them: what is the chain from business KPI down to offline eval, and where does it break?
technical: Three layers at three cadences: business KPIs (CSAT, deflection, cost per resolution) judge the initiative per quarter; online proxies (thumbs-down rate, retries, escalations, reopen rate) move per release; offline evals (groundedness, task success on a golden set) run per commit.
You cannot A/B test CSAT per pull request: it is too slow, too noisy and too diluted. Each layer exists because the layer above is unmeasurable at that cadence.

The chain is validated, never assumed: check that offline gains correlate with proxy gains release over release, and proxy gains with KPI movement quarter over quarter. A proxy that no longer correlates is a vanity metric.

Each layer needs a guardrail from the layer above. Shipping on offline scores alone invites Goodhart's law (when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure): the system learns the rubric, not the customer.

When the chain breaks (offline up, online flat), suspect in order: the golden set no longer represents live traffic, the judge has saturated near the top of its scale, or the proxy measures effort rather than outcome.
layman: A school steers weekly with mock tests, termly with report cards and yearly with university admissions. Mocks only matter because they historically predict the rest, and a mock everyone aces stops predicting anything.
usecases: Designing the eval program for a support assistant
Explaining to a sponsor why CI does not measure CSAT
Auditing whether a proxy metric is still connected to value
code:
per commit    offline eval    groundedness, task success on the golden set
per release   online proxy    thumbs-down, retries, escalation, reopen rate
per quarter   business KPI    CSAT, deflection, cost per resolution

validate the joints:
  offline gain -> proxy gain?   check release over release
  proxy gain   -> KPI gain?     check quarter over quarter

offline up, online flat -> golden set drifted, or the judge saturated
followups: How would you detect that the golden set has drifted away from live traffic?
Which single online proxy would you pick for a support bot, and why?
What does judge saturation look like on a dashboard?
redflags: Ships on offline scores with no online confirmation
Golden set never refreshed since launch
memory: Commit-time evals, release-time proxies, quarter-time KPIs, and the joints are checked, not assumed.

title: PEFT: When the Model Lacks Your Domain's Vocabulary
question: A foundation model keeps mishandling a highly specialised medical domain: rare terms fragment, abbreviations misread, the clinical register is off. Which adaptation technique is most appropriate, and why not prompting or RAG?
technical: The correct technique is fine-tuning, in practice Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT): continue training on domain text so the weights themselves learn the vocabulary, abbreviations and register absent from general training data.

Why not prompting: a prompt can carry definitions but cannot re-teach how the model reads; rare domain terms still tokenise into fragments the model has no learned feel for, and the ever-growing brief rides on every request's token bill.

Why not RAG: retrieval supplies documents to the same general-purpose reader. It fixes missing facts, not broken reading; the model misreads the retrieved medical text too. Vocabulary and register live in weights.

PEFT (LoRA and friends) freezes the base model and trains small low-rank adapters, typically well under 1% of parameters, so the adaptation fits modest hardware, ships as a small artifact, and can be swapped per domain at serving time.

Certification framing: options like prompt engineering, RAG, or larger context windows address knowledge and instructions; only fine-tuning addresses a vocabulary/jargon gap, and PEFT is the cost-appropriate form of it.
layman: A brilliant general reader handed a cardiology chart still reads it like a newspaper. Taping a glossary to the fridge (prompting) or handing over more charts (retrieval) does not change the reader; a short specialist course (fine-tuning) does.
usecases: Clinical, legal or scientific assistants where jargon density breaks a general model
Certification and interview questions on choosing an adaptation technique
Deciding between an adapter and a bigger prompt when quality plateaus
code:
the decision in one table:

gap                              fix
missing or changing facts        RAG (index outside the model)
loose behaviour, no data         prompt engineering
vocabulary, register, format     fine-tune (PEFT first)
whole language/domain shift      full fine-tune, if data + budget allow

PEFT sizing (7B-class model, LoRA rank 8 on attention):
trainable ~8.4M of 6.74B params  = 0.12%
followups: Where does the fine-tuning data come from, and who checks label quality?
How do you verify the adapter did not degrade general capability?
When would you extend the tokenizer vocabulary as well, and what does that cost?
redflags: Reaches for fine-tuning to inject facts that change weekly
Cannot explain why RAG does not fix a reading problem
No general-capability eval gating the adapted model's release
memory: Facts go in the index; vocabulary goes in the weights. A vocabulary gap is a weight gap: PEFT.

title: Fine-Tuning LLMs: Full, LoRA, QLoRA and the Forgetting Tax
question: Walk through the fine-tuning options for a 7B model on one 24 GB GPU: what full fine-tuning costs, what LoRA and QLoRA change, and what every fine-tune risks regardless of method.
technical: Full fine-tuning updates every weight: with Adam in mixed precision that is roughly 16 bytes per parameter (16-bit weights and gradients, 32-bit master copy and two optimiser moments), so a 7B model wants over 100 GB before activations: multi-GPU territory.

LoRA freezes the base and adds low-rank pairs A (d x r) and B (r x d) to chosen matrices; only those train. Rank 8 on attention is ~0.1% of parameters, so optimiser state collapses by the same factor and the result ships as a megabytes-sized adapter, swappable per tenant at serving time.
QLoRA additionally quantises the frozen base to 4-bit (~0.5 bytes per parameter, under 4 GB for 7B), making single-GPU fine-tuning routine; the adapters still train in 16-bit.

The forgetting tax: training only on specialist data erodes general capability, and freezing layers alone does not prevent it, because nothing in the loss defends old skills. Mitigations: replay (mix general data into the batches), a low learning rate, and gating release on a general eval suite as well as the domain one.

Data beats method: a few thousand clean, deduplicated, representative examples with verified labels outperform ten times the volume of scraped noise; hold out an untouched test set before anyone trains.
layman: A textbook you may not reprint: full fine-tuning re-typesets every page; LoRA tucks sticky notes into the margins; QLoRA does the same to a pocket edition. And any specialist course, however delivered, makes the student rusty at everything the course never mentioned unless they keep a day a week in general practice.
usecases: Domain adapters (legal, medical, house style) served per tenant
Single-GPU fine-tuning budgets and hardware sizing
Explaining to stakeholders why the specialised model must still pass the general test suite
code:
7B model, memory to train (weights + optimiser, activations extra):

full fine-tune   ~108 GB   every param, 16 B each
LoRA  (r=8)      ~13.9 GB  frozen 16-bit base + tiny adapter state
QLoRA (r=8)      ~4.1 GB   frozen 4-bit base  + tiny adapter state
                            ^ fits one 24 GB card with room to breathe

forgetting check, every run:
  eval(domain suite)   must rise
  eval(general suite)  must not fall
